en: Hara Oṃ.
Salutations to the venerable Guru Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
[Now begins the Śrī Vivekacintāmaṇi.]
[Now begins the first chapter]
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. [Verse]

Risen from churning the ocean of knowledge, endowed with the radiance of discernment, possessed of the esteemed wisdom of the learned, and united with the state of discrimination, he is a brilliant wish-fulfilling gem.
Having bowed to Ambikā, I shall provide an exposition in the language of the gods (Sanskrit) for that work composed by the one endowed with the glory of his own virtues, Śrī Karṇāṭaka-bhāṣā. || 1 ||
While the lord of serpents ruled over Rasātala and the wind-eating, hooded ones [ruled] over the sky, [the gods] remained there.
When Śakra is the ruler, wise men become enjoyers of sacrificial feasts; when the illustrious Liṅgarāja protects the earth, the serpents (rasāśana) become its guardians.
At Śrī Liṅgarāja, he bestows heaps of gold upon the assemblies of the learned.
Having taken up the golden mountain and placed it within his belly, the Creator attained the state of Hiraṇyagarbha.
The stream of the lovely sidelong glances of the illustrious Lord Liṅgarāja bestows love, gold, fearlessness, and the destruction of fear.
It was a marvel to the women, to the learned, to the friends who had sought refuge [with him], and to the multitude of wicked adversaries. || 4 ||
The *Vivekacintāmaṇi* was formerly compared with curiosity by the Lotus-born One to the *Cintāmaṇi*.
The elder Guru went to King Liṅga for the sake of the gods, while the younger one went to Hari.
This work concerning Śrī Liṅgarāja Umādhava brings joy and is to be cherished by the learned.
I write this *Tantrasāra* on the jewel of discriminative inquiry (*vivekacintāmaṇi*), composed by the heroic Nṛsiṃha.
Even without the study of all the scriptures, whoever [recites] this [hymn] dedicated to the venerable Liṅgarāja even once—
By reciting this, he certainly attains mastery over all arts and eloquence in assemblies. || 7 ||
The illumination of the work titled Vivekacintāmaṇi, composed in the Karṇāṭaka language.
It was produced by the polishing of the language of the gods, according to the opinion of the virtuous followers of the illustrious Liṅgarāja. (8)
Adorned with all the ornaments of the scriptures, he wears the crown of the illustrious Lord Liṅgarāja.
In the assembly of the King, he was a knower of all the Śiva Āgamas, like Kalādhara [the Moon] full amidst the stars. || 9 ||
And there are many treatises that expound upon all matters.

There is nothing equal to the venerable Liṅgarāja here, nor will there ever be. Thus ends the worship of the Pīṭhikā. Salutations to Śrī Śiva. [In prose: The worship of the pedestal is concluded. Salutations to the illustrious Śiva. In prose:

Out of love, I compose this great poetic work titled *Vivekacintāmaṇi* (The Wish-fulfilling Gem of Discernment)—an unfailing jewel whose name is proclaimed by the multitude of words from the Āgamas, Vedas, Purāṇas, and Śāstras for the benefit of many worlds, which reveals the well-established truth regarding the entire manifest universe—to you, O Śambhu-liṅga; therefore, listen to it and protect me. (Prose)

Having first saluted with mind, speech, and body the lineage of gurus— beginning with the Supreme Brahman known as Śambhu-liṅga, who is the foundational pillar for the commencement of the construction of many glorious worlds, and ending with the most excellent teacher Nirābhāri— I shall now describe the auspicious invocation characterized by prostration.
The completion of this treatise without obstacles, the setting in motion of a continuous succession of disciples and grand-disciples,
and the mental well-being of the audience— having determined these to be the fruits,
immediately thereafter [he is] endowed with beginningless, stainless, conscious form, supreme excellence, omniscience, and omnipotence.

"He who knows all things" refers to Śambhu, the soul of the *liṅga*, the creator of the entire phenomenal world— including the five forms (pañcamūrti) such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, as well as the five elements and so forth— who is endowed with omniscience as revealed by the Vedas.

Immediately following this, [there arises] the wealth of experience derived from the eloquent sayings of ancient authorities, as well as from the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas, which are rooted in both [Śruti and Smṛti], and which possess the status of the supreme authority based on their being composed by the Supreme Lord, whose authorship is revealed by the crest of the Vedas (Śruti), and which are in accord with the traditional transmission of the Āgamas.

In this very same way, having grasped those who hold "truth" to be such while actually gathering meanings of truth that have become either superior or inferior through their own mental fabrications— just like a person standing before a heap of jewels who perceives them as mere red dye— one should understand that mode of being and then sew it together with the thread of virtue.

May those seeking liberation, having effortlessly understood through this work— which has become like a fresh ornament for the neck— the manner in which the stability and movement of this world proceed, and having thereby attained realization, become fulfilled; thus [speaks] Nijaguṇaśivayogī.

He composed the treatise named *Vivekacintāmaṇi* and the *Saṃgraha*, using compositions in the form of ancient Karṇāṭaka verses. [Verse] The *Vivekacintāmaṇi* is a work on Vedānta philosophy attributed to Śaṅkarācārya. It consists of 578 verses divided into twenty-one chapters (*prakaraṇas*). The *Saṃgraha* is a summary of its contents. The text provided here indicates that these works were originally composed in the archaic Karṇāṭaka language.
The yogi of Śiva through his own innate qualities, meditating upon the supreme Śivaliṅga within the stainless interior of his own heart with all ritual offerings;
With a multitude of various vessels, the *Jñānacintāmaṇi* has here composed this *Prakaraṇa* for the sake of attaining right discernment through reasoning.
To the question, "How did he do that?", it is said in response: first, this world, which is perceived as the object of the external senses such as the eyes and so forth,
is [established] as an effect— just like a pot or similar objects composed of parts, characterized by a broad base, a belly, and so on.

By means of a Lord who acts as the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) like a potter, with merit and demerit— known as karma— acting as auxiliary causes (*sahakāri*) like the wheel and the rod, and with *māyā*— which consists of pure and impure elements resembling clay—
acting as the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), there arise various distinctions of worldly activity such as coming and going, pleasure and pain, and so forth.

It should be understood that [the world] is produced for the sake of the enjoyment and liberation of individual souls who are distinct from the Self; such is the intended meaning of this verse for the yogi of Śiva whose own qualities are thus described. [The Verse:]
The effects produced by a creator are "janya" (produced), because they are effects and possess birth.
All things that are created are said to have the Creator as their Lord.
For those things produced from the body are indeed born of volitional effort.
The Great Lord is the agent who brings about the counter-positive of prior non-existence.

Immediately following that, the Sāṃkhyas, Tārkikas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others who hold the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣin) declare: "In this matter, the primordial nature (prakṛti), atoms (paramāṇu), time (kāla), karma, inherent nature (svabhāva), necessity (niyati), the elements (bhūta), and their combinations are the creators of the world; there is no Lord (īśvara).
To that, the one who follows the doctrine of the Lord, the yogi Śivayogī, replies:

If it is argued that since everything from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) up to the conjunctions (*yoga*) is insentient by nature, agency is impossible without the superintendence of consciousness, and therefore the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses agency because it is sentient— no,
for that soul...

When it is asked how there could be the capacity for the contemplation of creating the world— given that [the soul] is tainted by defects such as limited knowledge, dependence on another, and lack of sovereignty— then,
since the aforementioned insentient matter and the individual soul cannot possibly be the agents of the earth and so forth, there must be one distinct from these who is omniscient.

Since an independent Lord must be postulated as the agent— because the earth and other effects, being insentient and living beings, cannot otherwise be established as having a cause— the existence of the Lord as the creator of all is proven by the means of knowledge known as *pariśeṣa* (presumption by elimination). Immediately thereafter, [one considers] such an effect in the form of this world...

When it is argued that [the world] must have many agents, like a chariot, we reply: that chariot is constructed by a single master according to the rule of a single craftsman; yet even a single task is not accomplished by multiple agents—each possessing a separate sense of being a knower and nourishing their own respective interests. Therefore, it must be admitted that the Lord of the Universe alone is the agent.
Furthermore, regarding the series of attributes of the Lord: since the arising of effects occurs at all times and in all places, because the Lord— who is the agent—
is eternal and all-pervasive, there can be no such [arising] without one who is capable of fully knowing the nature of those effects.

Thus, just as time— though formless— is the means for fruits, flowers, and so forth for the agent, the Lord, who possesses omniscience and omnipotence; likewise, because the Lord, the producer of all effects,
is stainless and dwells within the hearts of all living beings.

On the grounds that he is the regulator by means of external commands in the form of the Śrutis and Smṛtis, it is asserted that the Lord is the impeller of all. But how is this so? In the world, a potter or other agent regulates pots and the like which are distinct from himself; likewise, bodies and the like—which are regarded as other than himself—are regulated by him. In this same manner, the entire universe is regulated by the Lord.
By the scriptural statement "that which is to be restrained," there exists the Lord's nature as the self of all and his non-duality;

by this, the Lord's independence— due to being devoid of mother, father, and so forth— is established, as is his freedom from attachment and aversion in bestowing happiness and suffering according to the karma performed by individual souls.

The reality is that the conscious beings, such as humans, are incapable of creating the universe—consisting of space and other elements produced by the Lord—in any manner other than it actually exists; thus, the Lord’s status as the Sovereign of all remains firmly established.
This is the extent of what is being demonstrated.
The corroborative statements found in the *Mūla-atharvaṇaśiras*, the *Śikhātyāśramopaniṣad*, and others, as well as those spoken in the *Śiva Purāṇa* and other texts, are as follows. [Verse:]
In ancient times, certain sages who were seekers of liberation and exponents of Brahman,
their minds filled with doubt, reflected upon this matter in various ways.
What is the cause? From where have we been born? Or by what do we live?
Where is our foundation now established? By whom have we been made to flourish?
By whom do we constantly abide in various pleasures or otherwise?
And by whom have these arrangements been made for the one whose universal order is never transgressed?
Whether it be time, intrinsic nature, necessity, or chance that operates here.
The elements, the womb, the person, and yoga are indeed the sources of these great-souled ones;
for time and the like are insentient, while the self, though sentient, [is not the direct cause].

Because they were overcome by pleasure and pain and lacked self-mastery, they deliberated; then, following the yoga of meditation, they beheld the divine power which directly severs the bonds, though it is deeply hidden by the qualities (guṇas).
With their bonds severed by her, they beheld with divine vision the Great God, the Lord, the possessor of power, who is the cause of all;
he who indeed [is the source] of all causes, together with Time and the Self.
Immeasurable, he alone presides together with this power.

The treatises on epistemology [are] immediately thereafter [discussed], for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, among the individual active persons within the world— composed of sentient and insentient forms— created by the Supreme Lord.

When asked, "Which are those scriptures esteemed by the proponents? he first speaks thus: "The four Vedas—the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and Atharvaveda—which constitute the primary authorities, were composed by the self-existent Lord."
This is the intended meaning for one who is a yogin through the auspiciousness of his own qualities. To explain: there is a verse.
[The means of knowledge] subsisting on words, produced by non-different [causes], and distinct from what is to be approached.
I declare that the word which makes known the true meanings is the Veda.
That which is produced by the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence arising from words is considered "light" (laghu) among those things characterized by this definition.
The divisions of the Vedas are as follows: the Ṛgveda is divided into twenty-one branches, and the Yajurveda is divided into eleven branches.
The Sāmaveda is divided into a thousand branches, and the Atharvaveda is divided into nine branches; such is the established tradition.
Furthermore, as for the nature of Vedic statements, those Vedas exist in four distinct forms— namely, injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), mantras, and proper names—
and thus they continue to bring about the understanding of all dharmas, just like a king’s command.

The *vidhivāda* (injunction) is said to be that which, by negating the person [as an agent], makes known the duty of performing the dharma of cessation (*nivṛtti*), just as a bard establishes a divine matter. The *arthavāda* (explanatory passage) is like a teacher,
serving as a means for sacrifices and the like by way of illuminating the performance of sacrifices and the objects inherent therein.

A portion of the Veda is called a *mantra*. Just as one gives names to a mother and father, those names given to sacrifices and the like—such as *Jyotiṣṭoma*, *Vājapeya*, *Śyena*, and *Udbhid*—are *nāmadheya*s (proper names).
Through the fourfold [categories] beginning with injunction (*vidhi*), the manner of understanding their respective meanings is as follows.

In such injunctions as "One desiring heaven and the like should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites," that which is to be brought about (bhāvya) is the communication of the desire of a trustworthy person (āpta), in the form "Let this person here be prompted," which has as its instrumental cause the knowledge of the goat and so forth, and as its procedure (itikartavyatā) the act of incitement (prarocanā).

The bhāvanā directed toward one who desires heaven and the like, which has as its instrument sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, and is assisted by rites such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā, is to be applied to all injunctions and the like.
Furthermore, when it is asked, "What are the Vedāṅgas, which are the feet, hands, mouth, nose, eyes, and ears of the Veda? [the answer follows].
Prosody, ritual manuals, grammar, etymology, and likewise astrology;
And the Śikṣā—these, the wise say, are the six limbs of the Veda.
Metre is the feet of the Veda, while grammar is remembered as its mouth.
Furthermore, the meters of the mantras are of the types beginning with Triṣṭubh.
The calculation of the phonemes has been proclaimed by the sages;
indeed, [the works] composed by Āśvalāyana, Āpastamba, and Baudhāyana [are based upon it].
They know the Kalpa-sūtras, which are employed for the practical application of sacrificial rites.

This Śikṣā, which provides the determination of the udātta and other accents, brings about the grammatical perfection of words as they exist in both worldly and Vedic usage; for it is through this that one is taught the saṃhitā, pada, krama, and other recitation methods.
The science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra) is that which expresses the ascendant, planetary conjunctions, lunar days, and constellations.
Determining the proper time for sacrifices and other rites in this manner is highly praised.
The etymological explanation of Vedic words is called Nirukta.
The Upāṅgas are proclaimed to be the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Smṛtis.
I shall first state the characteristics of the Upāṅgas of the Vedas that have been mentioned, and thereafter [the characteristics of the Purāṇas].
Immediately following [the Vedas] are the Upavedas: Āyurveda, Arthaveda, and this Dhanurveda are thus declared.
The Gāndharvaveda and the four Upavedas have been thus described.

Among them, Āyurveda establishes longevity and health through the diagnosis of diseases, the symptoms of diseases, and treatments such as mantras and medicinal herbs. Arthaveda [establishes prosperity] by means of procuring sacrificial fees, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, offerings, and so forth.
The science of archery (*dhanurveda*) is the means for achieving the fourfold fruits consisting of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation;

furthermore, it provides the application of mantras, missiles, and other techniques for the purpose of conquering enemies. Indeed, the science of music (*gāndharvaveda*) is the classifier of the compositions of songs and so forth, based on the seven musical notes—*sa*, *ri*, *ga*, *ma*, *pa*, *dha*, and *ni*—found within the *Sāmaveda* and other texts.
It comes to be.
Immediately after the Upaniṣads. || Pa ||
The Śrī Rudra, Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Śvetāśvatara, and others.
Enveloped by the Kaivalya-sūkta, the Kālāgni, and the Kaṭha-vallī.
Likewise, Kātyāyana, Samāyukta, Brahmā, and Nārāyaṇa.
Haṃsa, Ukti, Paramahaṃsa, Bāṣkala, Brahma, and Binduka.
Likewise, there is the Āraṇyaka Upaniṣad known as the Amṛtabindu and the Arcarcanopaniṣad.
The Pañcabrahma Mahāmantra as well as the Jābāla Upaniṣad.
Then the Tejobindu, and after that the Vājasaneya.
The Bodhāyanīyas, the Āśvalāyanīyas, and the Maitrāyaṇīyakas.
And there are two [schools], namely the Sāṃkhyāyanīya and the Vāgurāyaṇīya.
It is also joined with the Śaunakīya [text] and is known as the Śivasaṃkalpa.
Hearing, valor, as well as the knowledge of Brahman and so forth.
For all the words that have been spoken are indeed set aside.
The Smṛtis follow immediately after:
the Smṛti of Manu is born from the three castes; the Hārītā Smṛti is born from Viṣṇu.
The Smṛti of Yājñavalkya, that of Jaimini, those spoken by Āṅgirasa and Yama,
the Āpastambīya, the Sāṃvartī, and the Smṛti composed by Kātyāyana.
The Bṛhaspati-smṛti as well as the Pārāśara-smṛti.
The Smṛti of Śaṅkha and Likhita belonging to Vyāsa, as well as the Sāradharas;
The Smṛti of Dakṣa, that spoken by Gautama, and those born of Śātātapa and Vasiṣṭha.
There are nineteen various treatises on Dharma;
among them, the law is primarily established by the *Manusmṛti* in the Kṛta Yuga,
while in the Tretā Yuga, the law is most highly esteemed according to the *Gautamasmṛti*.
In the Dvāpara age, the dharma of the Śaṅkha-Likhita Smṛti was likewise supreme;
in the Kali age, however, the dharma primarily practiced is that of the Pārāśara Smṛti,
concerning the conduct of castes, colors, and stages of life, as well as the division of inheritance and so forth.
These various and manifold eighteen divisions of legal procedure.
For in that regard, he indeed prescribes various distinctions of expiatory rites;
for there are castes distinguished as Kamata, Dravida, Karnata, and Andhra.
There are four castes named after their classes: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra.
Among them, there are sixteen sacraments (saṃskāras), including conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for ensuring a male child (puṃsavana), and the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).
The examination of the infant's limbs, the birth-rite, the naming ceremony,
the rite of taking the child out of the house, and the rite of first feeding with solid food are thus prescribed.
The Caula, Upanayana, Dvamdva, Mahānāmnī, and Mahāvrata;
likewise the Upaniṣad, Vivāha, Śobhana, and Mṛti.
Through these sixteen respectful duties followed by the Smārta Brahmins,
the ritual acts of a Brāhmaṇa are declared to be sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, as well as studying and teaching.
"Gift-giving and receiving—these two," thus he is endowed with the six duties.
One endowed with excellent qualities such as devotion to Śiva is called a Brāhmaṇa.
Sacrificing (*yajana*) is an activity conducive to the relinquishment of material substances directed toward a deity.
Officiating at a sacrifice (*yājana*) is the activity of a priest conducive to the performance of sacrificial rites.
Studying (*adhyayana*) is the utterance of the Veda by a disciple, dependent upon the utterance by a teacher.
Teaching.
The teacher's utterance that conforms to the student's utterance of Vedic sentences and so forth.

Giving (*dāna*) is a specific type of relinquishment (*tyāga*) residing in a substance to be given, such as a cow, which produces the destruction of one's own ownership and generates another's ownership;
and receiving (*pratigraha*) is the acceptance of a gift by the recipient through the payment of its price.
Immediately after the duties of a Kṣatriya. || pa. ||
The protection of subjects and the like, performing sacrifices, as well as the study of one's own Vedic recitation;
The protection of deer, the wicked, the malevolent, birds, and those who are hated;
the giving of food, the giving of clothing, and the bestowing of land and daughters in marriage. (Vṛtta)
The gift of a cow, gold, a two-faced vessel, a magnificent buffalo, and a white horse;
the great Meru-shaped gift, the Kalpavṛkṣa, and the glorious Mahādāna—these are the great gifts.
The purification of the place, time, recipient, and other factors for the sake of that gift—this entire wealth of devotion to Śambhu belongs to him who possesses it; he is a true Kṣatriya.

The designations in calculation are: one (1), ten (10), hundred (100), thousand (1,000), ten-thousand (10,000), lakh (100,000), ten-lakh (1,000,000), crore (10,000,000), ten-crore (100,000,000), hundred-crore (1,000,000,000), arbuda (10,000,000,000), and nyarbuda (100,000,000,000). ||1||

Kharva, Mahākharva, Padmaka, Mahāpadma, Kṣoṇi, Mahākṣoṇika, Śaṅkha, Mahāśaṅkha, Kṣitika, Mahākṣiti, and Kṣobha; ||2|| Nidhi, Mahānidhi, Sāgaraka, Mahāsāgara, Hari, Mahāharika, Śaṅkha, Mahāśaṅkha, and Phaṇika.
Phaṇi, Mahāphaṇi, Kramaka, Mahākrama. 3.
Immediately following: First position, Second position, Third position.
The fourth place, the fifth place,
the sixth place, and so on, up to the thirty-sixth place, are their respective values in sequence:
one, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a lakh (one hundred thousand), and ten lakhs.
Koṭi, ten koṭis (daśakoṭi), hundred koṭis (śatakoṭi), arbuda, nyarbuda, and kharva.
Mahākharva, Padma, Mahāpadma, Kṣoṇi, Mahākṣoṇi, Śaṅkha.
Mahāśaṅkha, Kṣiti, Mahākṣiti, Kṣobha, Mahākṣobha, and Nidhi.
The great treasure; the ocean; the great ocean; Hari; the great Hari; the serpent.
Mahāphaṇi, Kratu, and Mahākratu—these are the thirty-six locations.
Immediately following these are the names with a singular number such as *ekarūpabhūmi*, *saṃjñā*, *candra*, and so forth;
and in the Prākṛta language, those with dual names such as *beṃbeṃ* (meaning two), *dvi* (two), *dvandva*, and *yugma*.
Terms such as *yugula* (pair), *ubhaya* (both), *bāhu* (arm), *pāda* (foot), *pakṣa* (wing), and *nayana* (eye) are names for the number two.
Three times three, three; the eye of Hara; fire; city; group.
The names of the three categories beginning with "guṇa" are: four, gati, kaṣāya, veda, and varṇa.
Āśrama, Samudra, Saṃjñā, and so forth are the names of the four [elements]; Pañca is the fifth.
The faces of Śiva, the religious observances, the sense organs, the arrows, the objects of the senses, and the Pāṇḍavas.
"Bhūta" and so forth are the five names of the numbers. Six: Dravya, Ṛtu, Rasa.
The mouth of Skanda; the Vedāṅgas; ritual action; the vision of the castes.
The six names beginning with "Artha" are as follows: Sapta, Muni, Giri, and Rājyāṅga.

*Turaga*, *dhātu*, *sabhāṅga*, *svara*, *sāgara*, and so forth are names for the number seven. *Aṣṭa*, *vasu*, *diggaja*, *karman*, and so forth are names for the number eight. *Nava* [is a name for nine].
Hole, treasure, taste, planet, jewel, house, and so forth—these are the names for the nine numbers.
Bindu, Anusvāra, Śūnya, Nāsti, Gagana—these and others are the names of the bindu.

Having understood this designation which bestows all happiness, and having set aside further [calculation], one who multiplies the calculation and treats all things such as betel nuts as the standard measure writes down the number; this is auspicious.
In the acceptance or giving of goods based on increases, equal weights, or variations in color and quantity; and regarding gold,
the classification of its colors, and precious gems such as coral, jewels, diamonds, emeralds, and rubies.
Having individually observed [the examples] such as "kaṇaja," "causūtra," "parīkṣā," "mañca," and "adhirati."
Immediately following the measure of the *tulā*, ten *paṇas* constitute one *tulā*; four *gadyāṇas* constitute one *karṣa*.
Four *karṣas* make one *hala*; twenty *halas* constitute one *viṃśaka*.

Twenty *tulās* are said to be one *bhāra*. A quantity measured by ten *bhāras* is called an *ācita*. Thus, taking the *tulā* as the standard for camphor and other substances, a *kuñca* is one-fourth of a *māna*. Four *kuñcas* constitute a *kuḍava*.
Four *kuḍavas* make one *prastha*; two *prasthas* make one *vāha*.
Four of those make one āḍhaka; four āḍhakas make a droṇa; five droṇas make a bhāra.
The characteristics of a Vaiśya consist of counting grains and other commodities,
engaging in trade characterized by deliberation and execution, practicing agriculture and cattle-rearing, and performing duties such as devotion to the Sun.
He is called a Vaiśya.
Following the definition of the Śūdra: one who is engaged in service to the three castes, devotion to all the deities, and ritual worship; and who is humble—he is called a Śūdra.
The eighteen Purāṇas follow immediately after. || pa ||
The Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, and that named Bhāgavata.
The Mārkaṇḍeya, the Nāradīya, and that which is called the Āgneya.
The Bhaviṣya, Brahmavaivarta, Laiṅgya, and Vārāha [Purāṇas].
The one known as Skanda, Vāmana, Kūrma, Mātsya, and Gāruḍa;
Indeed, by our grace, the Purāṇa known as the Brahmāṇḍa [shall be revealed] to all of us.
The Blessed Vyāsa composed them in the excellent number of eighteen.
It has come to serve as a restatement of the meaning of lost Vedic branches.

The *Mahāvrata* itself, which prescribes practices such as the wearing of bone ornaments,
is the scripture of the mantrikas;
immediately following that is the scripture of mantras composed by Paraśiva, which constitutes a limb of liberation (*mokṣāṅga*).
He establishes the [four] stages of Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, and Jñāna. Regarding the demonstration of the Self—
furthermore, when it is asked what the nature of the Self is according to all other philosophical systems— it is stated that "the body alone is the Self."

The Cārvākas hold this view: since there is no cognition of "I" directed toward anything distinct from the body, the body alone is the self. Consciousness is a property produced in the body, just as the power of intoxication is produced from yeast and other ingredients;
in this regard, what is the cause? It is simply the combination of the elements (bhūtas), like the chewing of powdered camphor and betel leaf.

Just as that which produces redness [is not the body], so too this which produces consciousness [is not the body]; when the quality of consciousness has perished, there is the conventional usage "the living being is dead.

Some followers of the Cārvāka school hold that the senses are the self; other followers of the Cārvāka school, such as the Hiraṇyagarbhas, hold that the vital breath alone is the self. To this, the following reply is given regarding the body, the senses, and the vital breaths:
Because it is composed of the elements, the body is an object; because its perception is that of a subject, there is a distinction between the object and the subject.
Therefore, the body and so forth are not the Self. Immediately following this: the Self is indeed distinct from the body and other such things, yet it is limited by the body.
"Having come into being with a medium dimension, it is subject to contraction and expansion"—thus say the Jains.
In this regard, the reply is that the individual soul (jīva) must be non-eternal, because it possesses parts, like a jar.

The Buddhists maintain that consciousness alone is the self (*ātman*); the response to that is as follows: the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that consciousness itself is one. If it were said that the continuum of consciousness (*buddhi-saṃtati*) is the self, there would be the fault of impermanence (*anityatva*), because it would entail the postulation of infinite selves within a single body. The Kauyāma-Śākteyas maintain that bliss (*ānanda*) alone is the self.
To this, the reply is as follows: if the bliss produced by the worship of various means such as pills (*guṭikā*) or sandals (*pādukā*) were the Self, it would follow that the Self is non-eternal;

even if it were eternal, if it were distinct from consciousness (*cit*), it would follow that it is insentient (*jaḍa*); and if that bliss were of the nature of consciousness and eternal, it would result in entering the domain of other philosophical systems. Therefore, the Self has the dimension of an atom (*aṇu-parimāṇa*), resides in the center of the navel, and is not all-pervading (*vibhu*).

Regarding the argument that "the soul is not atomic because [otherwise] its departure and movement would be impossible," the Pāñcarātrikas and Bhāgavatas offer this reply: [If the soul were atomic,] it would follow that it is insentient and imperceptible; furthermore, the postulation of an infinite number of souls would entail unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, the soul is not atomic. As for the common folk, they hold that the self consists of the body, sons, and so forth. To that, the following is the reply:

Because it would entail impermanence, the authors of the Mīmāṃsā school, such as the venerable Bhaṭṭa, the Prābhākara masters, and others, maintain that the self— established by its own means of valid cognition— is distinct for each body; to this,
the reply is that there is complexity (gaurava) in the case of the self's multiplicity, and none in the case of its unity.
It must be stated that the pleasure, pain, and so forth experienced by Devadatta are not experienced by Yajñadatta; otherwise,

there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of one and the same self, while residing in this body, remembering pleasures experienced in the bodies of other births, [if it were not for the fact that] the difference in bodies acts as an obstacle.
If this is argued, then there is no contingency of Devadatta— who resides in a body distinct from Yajñadatta’s body—
possessing such a cognition of pleasure, because of the difference between the two bodies;
and since it is simpler to hold that "the self is the cognition itself" in the statement "cognition accompanied by the self is the self," the self is indeed cognition.

The Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas maintain that because it possesses a great dimension, the self is comparable to space; yet, although it is as inert as a stone, it becomes endowed with the attributes of consciousness through conjunction with the mind.
The responses to these have already been given by means of the refutation of the Mīmāṃsaka position; however, there is a specific distinction here:

it is their view that the Supreme Self must be insentient (*jaḍa*). This is because [if it were sentient], it would be distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), like a jar. By this, the Pāñcarātras are also refuted;
for the Supreme Self as conceived by them is not knowable through the Vedas, since it is known only through the mark of its effects (*kāryaliṅga*).

Nor is the individual soul (jīva) known through the Veda as such; for it is known through direct perception as "I. Nor is the difference between the two known through the Veda; for that too is known through direct perception as "I am not the Lord. Therefore, the identity of the individual soul and Brahman is what is known through the Veda, because it cannot be reached by any other means of knowledge. Furthermore, the identity of the individual soul and Brahman is not their [respective] essential nature (svarūpa), because [if it were], that [identity] would be known [simply] upon knowing them.

If that [reality] is already determined, how can it be said to be "knowable through the Vedas"? It is because of the delusion of duality acquired from beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that it is not known; just as the moon’s size of one *prādeśa* is not known due to delusion, nor its vast extent of many thousands of *yojanas*.

The Sāṃkhyas and Pātañjalas [hold that] the Self is pure consciousness (asaṅga-cinmātra), characterized by being knowable through the true scriptures, extensiveness, and unity. To this, we offer the following reply: there is the conceptual complexity (kalpanā-gaurava) of postulating a manifold nature for the Self based on the perceived connection with agency and so forth, as in the thought "I am the doer. As for the Self...

The Vedāntins declare that the Self is pure consciousness alone (*jñaptisat-mātra*). Those established in the Pāśupata, Kāpālika, and Mahāvrata systems maintain that the Self is eternal, all-pervading consciousness (*nityavyāpakacaitanya*). The proponents of the Māntra school assert that the Self consists of eternal, all-pervading knowledge and action (*jñānakriyārūpa*). Thus, they are renowned as distinct [traditions].
Immediately following the exposition on liberation, when it is asked what the definition of liberation as propounded by all [other] disputants is,
the Cārvākas say that liberation is simply death. Others hold that liberation is the progressive upward movement into the midst of the transcendent ether.

Thus say the Jains. The Buddhists hold that liberation is precisely the continuum of pure consciousness, free from connection with pleasure, pain, and the like. The Kauyāmas (? maintain that liberation is the accomplishment of traveling to all worlds, such as Ākāśa and others. The Śākteyas hold that liberation is the attainment of bliss.

The Pāñcarātrikas maintain that liberation (mokṣa) is indeed a state of being dissolved within the primordial nature (prakṛti), which has Vāsudeva as its essence, by attaining proximity to Him without any loss of one's own essential nature (svarūpa). The worldly people (laukikas), however, hold that liberation is simply the state of abiding in happiness, free from the suffering of disease and the like, through union with sons, wives, and others, both here and in the hereafter.
Ordinary people believe that liberation is simply the attainment of heaven and other realms free from death;

the followers of Karma-mīmāṃsā hold that liberation is the persistence of the self like a stone, characterized by the destruction of the twenty-one forms of suffering, namely the six cognitions, the six sense organs, the six objects, pleasure, pain, and the body.

Liberation (*mokṣa*) is either the destruction of all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) existing immediately after the arising of the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*), or it is the absence of the arising of any specific quality co-located with the destruction of specific qualities that occurs immediately after the arising of the direct realization of reality— this being subsequent to the direct realization of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

The Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas maintain that liberation (*mokṣa*) is characterized by the occurrence of a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) coexisting with the same substratum at the time when all previously arisen specific qualities have been destroyed.

Furthermore, the moderns [the Naiyāyikas] hold that liberation (mokṣa) is the absence of specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa-śūnyatva), characterized by co-location with the destruction of those qualities as qualified by the time subsequent to the direct realization of reality (tattva-sākṣātkāra).
The Sāṃkhyas, however, maintain that liberation is simply the destruction of ignorance (avidyā) produced by the discrimination between primordial matter (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa).

The followers of Yoga and Patañjali maintain that liberation is precisely the destruction of adventitious ignorance through the dissolution of the mind attained by the power of yogic practice. The Vedāntins hold that liberation is simply the cessation of empirical bondage, which is the goal to be accomplished for the sake of security, arising from the knowledge of the single reality of Brahman and the Self.

Furthermore, regarding the state of being achievable through common means for security: when that [security] exists, there is the existence of what is not to be destroyed; and in its absence, there is the existence of its opposite.

This is because the Mīmāṃsakas have stated this with respect to the prior non-existence of suffering that is to be remedied by expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). Having relegated the status of being a Lord (*īśvaratva*) elsewhere, on the grounds that it is merely lordship over a continuous flow (*pravāha*).

The Pāśupatas hold that liberation consists in the self abiding in mere consciousness (*jñapti-mātra*). Those established in the great vow (*mahāvrata*) of the Kāpālikas maintain that transmigratory existence is the very conceit of agency, and thus liberation is the self’s functioning through the mere consciousness that is the opposite of that [conceit]. Of the self...

The proponents of the Māntra school explain that liberation (*mokṣa*) is the attainment of equality with the Supreme Lord, who transcends the six paths consisting of the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*), the path of words (*padādhvan*), the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*), the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), and the path of limited powers (*kalādhvan*).
Regarding the distinction between other philosophical systems:

among the disputants (*vādins*), the Cārvākas, Jains, Buddhists, Mīmāṃsakas, and Sāṃkhyas alone are proponents of non-theism (*anīśvaravādins*). All disputants other than these are proponents of theism (*seśvaravādins*). Furthermore, among the disputants...
The Cārvākas and others are proponents of difference, whereas the Vedāntin alone is a proponent of non-difference.
Furthermore, among all the treatises here, there are fourteen branches of knowledge (vidyās). [End of page.]
The Vedāṅgas, the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive Nyāya;
The Purāṇas and the Dharmaśāstras—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
An Investigation of the Sūtra:
Immediately following this, among the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), Mīmāṃsā is distinguished;
consisting of twenty chapters, it is divided into two parts by virtue of its exposition of ritual action (*karman*) and its meaning. Within that [second part]...
The first part, consisting of twelve chapters in the form of Jaimini’s Sūtras, serves as the exposition of the agent and the action;
it includes such topics as "Now, therefore, dharma" (*athāto dharma*) and the various sections on worldly and Vedic matters, along with the *Anvāhārya* [ceremony].

Due to the thousands of methods for the investigation of perception (*darśana*), it is well known as Pūrva-mīmāṃsā. Therefore, Śabarasvāmin composed the *Śābara-bhāṣya* on the collection of Jaimini’s sūtras.

Immediately thereafter, the venerable Bhaṭṭācārya composed one school of thought, the Bhāṭṭa, in the form of a Vārttika on the Mīmāṃsā Śāstra. Subsequently, the teacher Prabhākara, a disciple of the venerable Bhaṭṭācāryas, [composed] [a commentary] on the Śābara Bhāṣya.
After formulating the Prābhākara school as a distinct philosophical system,

[the author] subsequently composed the *Uttaramīmāṃsā*, consisting of eight chapters in the form of the *Balabhadra-Vyāsa-sūtra*, which establishes the nature of the deity and Brahman as its subject matter.

The first four chapters are called the *Devatākāṇḍa* (Section on Deities); within that, Balabhadra Rāma has established that the definition of a deity is like that of a mantra. Following that, the subsequent four chapters are said to constitute the *Brahmakāṇḍa* (Section on Brahman).

In that [work], the Śārīrakabrahmamīmāṃsābhāṣya, which establishes the identity of Brahman and the Self, was composed by the venerable teacher Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda. Subsequently, the Vivaraṇa-śāstra was composed by the venerable Vivaraṇācārya, whose feet are served by all teachers.
Furthermore, the Vedānta-śāstra itself is primarily designated as the "Exposition" (Vivaraṇa).
When it is asked what the sequence of topics concerning Vedānta is, and what the expansion of that Vedānta-śāstra is like,
[the answer is: at the commencement of a treatise, there are the benediction, the salutation, and the indication of the subject matter.
The three [kings] performed auspicious rites.
The characteristics of exposition consist of the application of words, word-meanings, and sentences, as well as questions and answers; these are the five characteristics of exposition.
The characteristic of logical connection [is as follows]:
The five characteristics consist of the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), the qualified (viśeṣya), the agent (kartṛ), the object (karman), and the connection with the action (kriyānvaya);

the four ancillaries (anubandhacatuṣṭaya) consist of the relation, the delimiting form of that relation (saṃbandhatāvacchedakarūpa), the appearing relation (abhāsamānavaiśiṣṭya), and the counter-positive (pratiyogi) which is the qualifier.
The qualificand (viśeṣya) is that which follows the suffix (*anuyogin*) appearing [in the word]. The agent (*kartṛ*) is one who possesses an effort conducive to the effect;
the object (*karman*) is that which possesses a fruit produced by an action inherent in another.
Grammarians (*śābdika*) maintain that the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix is "the substratum of the operation conveyed by the verbal root," namely, the agent.
The four prerequisites of the scripture—namely, the subject matter (*viṣaya*), the purpose (*prayojana*), the relationship (*saṃbandha*), and the qualified student (*adhikārī*)—are as follows:

among these, the subject matter of the scripture is precisely the identity of the individual soul and Brahman (*jīvabrahmaikya*); the relationship between the scripture and Brahman is that of the expounder and the expounded (*pratipādaka-pratipādya-bhāva*).
The sole purpose is the attainment of eternal bliss through the cessation of ignorance, which is the source of all suffering and grasping.
As for the definition of the qualified seeker: only one who is endowed with the fourfold qualifications is eligible.

The fourfold means [to knowledge] immediately following [this inquiry] are: discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter, the attainment of the six qualities beginning with tranquility (śama), and the desire for liberation. Among these, the Self, whose nature is consciousness, is eternal.

The discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities (*nityānityavastuviveka*) is the discernment that everything else besides that [Brahman]—the entire realm of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*)—is indeed false.

Furthermore, all enjoyment of objects in this world and the next, such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and women, is non-eternal because it is produced by karma; thus, from its acquisition until its final consumption, it is characterized by a sequence of transience.

The nature of suffering consists in that which is obtained through great exertion, distaste, and so forth; the absence of mental expansion [toward such things] is detachment from the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter. The accomplishment of the six qualities beginning with tranquility (*śama*) is called the perfection of tranquility and the rest. The longing for innate union (*sahaja-sāyujya*) alone is proclaimed as the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*). Immediately thereafter—

The six qualities beginning with tranquility (*śama*) are indeed tranquility, self-restraint (*dama*), forbearance (*titikṣā*), cessation (*uparati*), faith (*śraddhā*), and concentration (*samādhi*). Among these:
tranquility is the calming of the mind; self-restraint is the control of the senses;
and forbearance is the endurance of anger regarding all actions.
The complete cessation of attachment as prescribed, and trust in the Guru and the Vedas.
Faith in this instruction of the guru arises from the firmness of mind attained through meditative concentration (samādhi).

Immediately thereafter, one should [instruct] according to rule a disciple who has sought refuge, who is devoted to the study of Vedānta and intent upon its realization, and who possesses the characteristics of a [worthy] guru.
Furthermore, he who, by imparting instruction on reality such that no further doubt arises, dispels ignorance,
is called a *guru*;
this is the defining characteristic of service to a *guru*.
Immediately following this, it is asked: what is the nature of the service performed by one who possesses the qualification of the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*)?

It is said to be fourfold, consisting of the presence of the *āpta*, the limbs (*aṅga*), the place (*sthāna*), and the true state (*sadbhāva*). Among these, *āptatā* (trustworthiness) is simply conduct that is favorable toward the guru. *Aṅga* consists of such acts as washing the guru’s feet. [The rest] consists of protecting the guru’s house, fields, and so forth.
The "place" (sthāna) is said to be the Guru himself as the manifest Paraśiva; "true being" (sadbhāva) is simply faith.

Following that, there is the distinction of qualified practitioners (adhikārin), who are categorized separately as those belonging to the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍin), the section on devotion (bhaktikāṇḍin), and the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍin).

There are three types of qualified practitioners. Among them, one who possesses the sense of "I" and "mine" (*ahaṃkāra* and *mamakāra*) regarding household duties and the like is called a practitioner of the *karmakāṇḍa*. One who performs all actions with the understanding that they are offered to the Lord is blessed and is called a practitioner of the *bhaktikāṇḍa*.
One who possesses the knowledge that "I am the witness of all actions" is called a knower of the section on knowledge (jñānakāṇḍin).

Following these, there are five types of qualified practitioners: the ritualist (karmī), the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), the practitioner (abhyāsī), the one with direct experience (anubhavī), and the one who has ascended (ārūḍha).

There are five types of practitioners, each succeeding one being superior to the previous. Among them, the *karmī* is a person who, through a state of delusion (*mūḍhabhāva*), adopts actions according solely to his own caste; after a hundred births, such a person attains liberation. One who, having realized that the world is real, is devoted to external ritual action, [attains liberation] after three births.

The seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) is one who desires release. The practitioner (*abhyāsī*) is one who, realizing that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is false like a dream, is engaged in internal practices such as meditation and attains liberation after two births.
The experiencer (*anubhavī*) is one who, while depending on worldly activity, is intent upon discrimination (*viveka*) and attains liberation in a single birth.
Having realized that all transformations are unreal through self-knowledge, he was immediately liberated; yet, having ascended,
he subsequently approached the venerable Guru by way of inquiry as to what the root of this lotus-stalk of the world might be, [in order to fulfill] the threefold qualification.

Having heard that one who has attained the knowledge of Brahman has achieved liberation; that another, having perceived the impermanence of the body and other such things, abandoned the desire for enjoyments and, having approached a venerable guru, became a knower of reality and is now engaged in providing instruction to his own disciple as a means to accomplish liberation.
Being a knower of the Self by chance and thereby attaining Nirvana—such is the one [liberated].

Those liberated through discrimination (*viveka*), dispassion (*virakti*), and the course of destiny (*daivagati*) are each [considered] qualified candidates (*adhikārins*). [Next is] the characteristic of the eight types of gurus.

Immediately thereafter, the venerable gurus themselves, according to the distinction of the qualifications of their practitioner-disciples, are of three types: the awakener (*bodhaka*), the knower (*vedaka*), and the prohibited guru (*niṣiddhaguru*). A verse [on this]:
The awakener, the knower, and likewise the prohibited guru.
The one who inspires desire, the indicator, the reciter, the performer,
and the preceptor— thus, O Lord, you exist as eight kinds of gurus.
Among them, he who awakens [the disciple] to the words and meanings of the scriptures by means of an exposition characterized by the five marks (pañcalakṣaṇa) is [the Guru].

The "awakening teacher" (*bodhakaguru*). In this context, a word (*pada*) is that which possesses either the function of primary denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The meanings of words (*padārtha*) are those things understood from a word by means of its function. For example, in the expression "fish in the Gaṅgā," the meaning of the word *gaṅgā* is the river-current by primary denotation; whereas in the expression "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," [the meaning is the bank] by the function of indication.

The phrase "the meaning of the word *gaṅgā* is the bank" is an instance of syntactic construction (*yojanā*). A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of words possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and contiguity (*sannidhi*); the communication of the sentence-meaning through that [collection] is syntactic construction (*yojanā*), which occurs upon the absence of certain words.
The non-experience of the sentence-meaning by a word that has been employed [in a context] consists of:
(1) the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) of that word together with that word;

(2) the fitness (*yogyatā*), which is the sentence-meaning having as its counter-positive the meaning of another word that is the intended object of the single word’s meaning; and (3) the immediate presentation of the counter-positive of the sentence-meaning.
The collection: Verse.

Truth, knowledge, the supreme Brahman, bliss, devoid of attributes, most excellent, non-different from the individual soul (jīva), the creator of the world, and the sustainer and destroyer of the world.

In such passages, having understood the unity of the six [sentences] through either the unity of the sentences themselves or the unity of the meaning of the sentences, one joins them together regarding the meaning of the whole;

for one who doubts the meaning of the word *brahman*, the word "What is Brahman? constitutes the question, and the previously stated sentence that removes the doubt which is the seed of the question constitutes the answer.
The teacher who provides instruction endowed with these characteristics is the *bodhaka-guru*. The teacher who reveals reality is the *vedaka-guru*.

The one who bestows happiness in this world through practices such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), but causes suffering in the next world, is the prohibited (*niṣiddha*) teacher.
The teacher who bestows happiness in both this world and the next by instructing in meritorious deeds is the *kāmya-guru*, [acting] by way of discernment (*viveka*).
The indicative guru (*sūcaka-guru*) bestows excellent qualities such as tranquility and self-restraint;
the expressive guru (*vācaka-guru*) bestows love for the Self by demonstrating the falsity of sense objects;
and the causal guru (*kāraṇa-guru*) bestows the knowledge of the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (*jīva*) by means of dispelling doubts.
The appointed Guru, who bestows eternal liberation and receives the devotion of his disciples,
[is followed] immediately thereafter by a certain qualified person among the Sadguru and the good disciple, [who is consumed] by the fire of the threefold suffering.

Being burnt, his mind became agitated, and he reflected: "Who am I? What is my cyclic existence (saṃsāra)? By what means was it obtained, and by what means shall it be brought to an end? Having thus reflected, he prepared offerings of leaves, flowers, fruits, sacrificial fuel (samidh), and so forth.

Having become a human being endowed with excellent qualities such as knowledge, discipline, and detachment, and having approached the venerable Guru, one performs the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-namaskāra) in conjunction with the ground, preceded by the eight mantras beginning with "The eternal, peaceful Consciousness," touching the two feet, the two hands, the two arms, the chest, and the forehead.
Having bowed down, then rising up again, placing his lotus-like hands upon his head out of fear and devotion, accepting the state of a servant, displaying his wretchedness,
and praising him with joy;

O Blessed One, O True Guru, since you possess the perfection of the six qualities— knowledge, dispassion, strength, sovereignty, fame, and splendor— by what means may my bondage to worldly existence be removed without exertion?
To make such a request is itself the disciple’s formal approach according to the rules.
The sequence of instruction: immediately thereafter, having observed the qualification of the disciple who has approached him and having looked upon him with a compassionate glance, [the teacher],
saying "Do not be afraid," places the 'Bestower of Fearlessness' (abhayakara) upon his head, [establishing it] for him through scripture, reasoning, and direct experience.

The instruction of the venerable guru, which is the illumination of awakening, consists solely in generating the knowledge that "having abandoned the notion of the body and so forth as the self, you yourself are the supreme Brahman in the form of pure consciousness."
Furthermore, in the sequence of instruction, there are three modes of teaching: the brief statement (uddeśa), the definition (lakṣaṇa), and the examination (parīkṣā); this is the verse on that point.

An *uddeśa* (enunciation) consists in the mention of a thing by name alone, which produces a mere mental apprehension; it is the characteristic of a thing that produces a cognition delimited by the very property that serves as its defining condition (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*).

Establishing the attainment of excellence within the object of observation, the fortunate Parīkṣā, possessing pure speech and virtuous reflection, being wise through his own qualities, thus speaks of the threefold nature of the treatise with distinction.
That which merely mentions the object intended to be established by oneself is *uddeśa* (enunciation).

A definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is a statement that expresses a property co-extensive with the delimitor of the state of being the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), which resides in the object to be defined (*lakṣya*), just as in the case of "a cow is that which possesses a dewlap and so forth. Examination (*parīkṣā*) is the investigation conducive to establishing the validity of the definition for the object to be defined.

The uncommonness (*asādhāraṇatva*) of a property consists in its being co-extensive with the delimiting condition of the locus (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*). Nor does it follow that the exclusion of [the subject] from others than the jar (*ghaṭetara-vyāvṛtti*) would also be a definition because of its co-extensiveness with that [delimiting condition]; for this is not an acceptable consequence, as it would entail the fault of non-distinction from the probandum (*sādhya*), [in the case of the inference]: "The jar is distinct from others."

It should be stated that this is based on the inference: "because it possesses exclusion from what is other than a jar. Regarding the position that a definition is a distinguishing property (*vyāvartaka-dharma*), the qualification "being distinct from a property that is exclusively positive (*kevalānvayi*) in its exclusion" must be added;

however, regarding the position that a definition is a property that does not serve as a basis for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-aprayojaka-dharma*), it need not be added, since even exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and the like [are included].
Since a definition serves as the basis for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), there are three defects:
under-extension (*avyāpti*), over-extension (*ativyāpti*), and impossibility (*asaṃbhava*).
Under-extension is the state of being the counter-positive of an absence that co-exists with the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*).
Over-extension (*ativyāpti*) consists in being present in that which is to be defined (*lakṣya*), while also being present in that which is not to be defined (*alakṣya*).

The impossibility [of a definition] consists in a property contradictory to the delimiting condition of the object to be defined (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*). According to the principle that "the supreme Brahman known as Sadāśiva possesses a definition—namely, the agency in the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world—which is free from the three defects and serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that facilitates the establishment of the reality," [it is stated as follows]: [Verse]
Having correctly discerned the characteristic, the yogi, designated by his own qualities, [attains success].
He undertakes the examination of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) for the sake of establishing his desired position.
Regarding the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
God, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), time, the agent, the instrument, and so forth are the causes of valid cognitive knowledge;
among these, that which is the uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇahetu*) serving as the substratum for the operation resulting in the production of knowledge is alone the *pramāṇa*.
The classification of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vibhāga*): immediately following [the definition],
there are the means of valid cognition consisting of perception, inference, verbal testimony, comparison, postulation, non-apprehension, probability, and tradition.

Since the establishment of real entities [requires] eight means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), among them, the sense organ (*indriya*)— which is the instrument for the direct perception of jars and so forth—

is the means of valid cognition called perception (*pratyakṣa*). Smoke and so forth, which produce the cognition of fire and so forth that is the counter-positive of an absence consisting in the non-occurrence [of smoke] in the locus of smoke and so forth, [are the means of valid cognition called inference].
Knowledge is inference. The members of the inference just described are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*udāharaṇa*).
The statement that makes known the relationship between the subject and the property to be proven—such as "the mountain possesses fire"—is the proposition.
The knowledge characterized by [the reason] is the indicator; "because it possesses smoke," ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*), is the reason. "Whatever possesses smoke... [is the example].

The statement "That [place] possesses fire, like a kitchen" is the example (*udāharaṇa*). This triad of statements constitutes the syllogism (*nyāya*), which is a verbal expression produced by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) for the purpose of establishing the intended meaning.
This is the means of valid cognition consisting of scripture (*āgama-pramāṇa*).

Scriptural testimony (*āgama*) is a word that generates a cognition of a relation which is the intended object and stands in the relation of counter-correlativity to the meanings of the words uttered together; or, scriptural testimony is the statement of a reliable person regarding a matter as it actually is,
as in the case of Devadatta, who does not eat during the day.
The fact that corpulence cannot otherwise be accounted for by the eating at night is the means of valid cognition known as *dṛṣṭārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is seen).

Upon hearing that "Devadatta, who is alive, is not in the house," the knowledge that he must be elsewhere is the means of valid cognition known as *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard). [And] "the *gavaya* is similar to a cow" [is an example of analogy].
After hearing the words of the forest-dweller, for the city-dweller who has gone to the forest,

the perception of the individual substance of a gavaya— characterized by its similarity to a cow— produces the knowledge of the function of denotation in the form of the relationship between a name and the named, namely "this is what is expressed by the word *gavaya*"; this is comparison (*upamāna*) existing on the ground.

The non-apprehension of a jar, assisted by the following reasoning, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its absence: "The cognition 'the jar is not here' is produced by the knowledge of the jar's absence; for if a jar were present here, it would have been perceived just like the ground; therefore, there is an absence of perception. This is the case when [the number] is one thousand.

The knowledge that "the number one hundred is possible" is the *sambhava* (possibility) means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The worldly report, "A yakṣa dwells in this banyan tree," which is a cognition concerning a yakṣa, is the *aitihya* (tradition) means of valid cognition.
Among those aforementioned means of valid cognition, for the Cārvākas, perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone is the single means of valid cognition.

The Jains and Buddhists maintain that verbal testimony, inference, and so forth lack validity because they produce a doubt with a predominant alternative; thus, activity and the like arise from a doubt characterized by a predominant alternative.
Now, in the system of the Vaiśeṣikas, there are two means of valid cognition: perception and inference. Indeed, this is the position of the Vaiśeṣikas.

If it is argued that if verbal testimony were not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), there would be no cognition of an object from words, we say: it would indeed not exist [as an independent source], but rather by way of inference (*anumāna-vidhayā*). For we do not deny the validity of verbal testimony; rather, we subsume it under inference. Thus:
The word "cow" is preceded by the cognition of its object, like the word "existence," because it is a word "cow" that requires the word "existence."

That which is not thus is not thus, as for example space. [The Sāṃkhyas argue: "Cowness exists, because it is recalled by a word that possesses expectancy and so forth conducive to the cognition of its own substratum's existence through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), like a pot; and because it is recalled by the word 'cow' occurring in syntactic contiguity with the word 'exists', like the eye. This is the position of the Sāṃkhyas.
The three means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) are perception, inference, and scripture; we shall establish the reasoning for this further on.
For the Naiyāyikas, there are four means of valid cognition: perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony.
Regarding the validity of verbal testimony as a distinct means of cognition, the reasoning is as follows: there is a recollection of the word-meanings produced by the words [of a sentence].

Only the word-meaning as an existent entity (*svarūpasat*) is useful for the cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya*), not as something already known, because there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for such knowledge;

furthermore, if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that syntactic relation would be cognized even for a meaning not recalled by words, since one could still apprehend its being "recalled" [by other means].
Therefore, in a sentence such as "the cow exists," it must be accepted that the cow is heard as possessing existence, but it is not inferred.

Having observed the usage "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) and "it is to be reflected upon" (*mantavya*), and because [the object] denoted by the root *śru* (to hear) can also be the delimitor of the capacity [of the word], the Prābhākaras hold that there are five means of valid cognition, including presumption (*arthāpatti*).
In their view, Vedic sentences are authoritative, as are worldly sentences.

The ascertainment that the words which convey the meaning of awakening (bodhitārtha) are not unestablished— due to their being expectant (*sākāṅkṣatva*) and so forth— and that they possess the quality of being "not stated by another" (*aproktatva*), which consists in their being uttered as having the knowledge of this sentence-meaning as their object, is also a cause for verbal cognition (*śābda*). Therefore, [it is not the case that] that which has the property of a single word-meaning as its subject...

Inference (*anumiti*) is the cognition of the connection with another object. Since such a cognition is possible even when there is already a proof (*siddhi*), it is something distinct; however, because it apprehends what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitvāt*), it is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is because, for that class of qualified cognitions delimited by its specific nature, it possesses the property of occurring subsequent to a certainty (*niścaya*) of the same form.

Because a subsequent cognition of the same class that apprehends what has already been apprehended is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) since it grasps what is already grasped. For this very reason, although successive instances of continuous perception (*dhārāvāhika-pratyakṣa*) occur after the apprehension of an identical form, they do not suffer a loss of their status as valid cognitions. However, there is indeed a loss [of validity] for those [cognitions] arising from the experience of an identical form [when that form has already been previously apprehended].

If it is argued that, according to the view of the elders (gurūṇām), the determination of the intended meaning (*tātparya-niścaya*) regarding the recollections is the cause of the cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya-dhī*), because otherwise— even when there is a determination that the phrase "pot-objectness" (*ghaṭa-karmatva*) has another primary purpose— the cognition of the relation "objectness belonging to the pot" (*ghaṭīya-karmatva*) would result from the sentence "the pot" (*ghaṭam*).
At a time when there is a certainty regarding the absence of intentionality directed toward the coreferential connection of a jar and so forth as the objecthood (karmatā),

even if there is a certainty that the jar’s objecthood and so forth are intended in the manner of "knowability" (prameyatva) etc., the cognition of the coreferential connection "the objecthood belongs to the jar" does not arise; therefore, [the cause] is the [certainty] having as its qualifier the intentionality directed toward a cognition of the coreferential connection of the jar as the objecthood.

Since the cognition of the speaker's intention (*tātparya-dhī*) functions as a cause precisely by virtue of its being indeterminate, the sentence-meaning does not enter into it; thus, even when there exists a certainty regarding another sentence— which is in fact identical in its phonetic sequence— that the speaker intends it to convey meanings such as "the pot" being the object (*karmatva*) at a later time.
Since the status of being directed toward that [the jar] is not ascertained— either because it is not certain due to the inclusion of ignorance whose nature is manifested by the sentence being heard,
or because it is already established— the cognition of the syntactic connection such as "this is the objecthood belonging to the jar" cannot arise unless it is distinguished [from other objects].

One must accept that the ascertainment of the intentionality (*paratva*) toward the objecthood of the pot (*ghaṭakarmatva*) and so forth, residing in the respective sentence as its locus, is the cause for the cognition of the respective syntactic connection (*anvaya*).

And thus, it is appropriate that at that time (*tadātva*), it is precisely the cognitions of context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth—which serve as the causes for that [ascertainment]—that constitute the specific instances of consciousness (*vijñānavyakti*). This is because such a [causal] relation must necessarily be postulated.

Because it possesses the property of being antecedent [to the cognition]. For this very reason, even in cases such as "Bring the *saindhava*," the cognition that the word refers to salt is not the cause of the cognition of the connection with salt and so forth;
rather, it is the recollection (*pratisaṃdhāna*) of the context (*prakaraṇa*), such as eating, which is intended to have that meaning.

Setting aside that which contradicts the established tenets of logic (*nyāyasiddhānta*), the knowledge of the intended meaning (*tātparya*)—which is intended as the cause for generating the comprehension of the sentence-meaning—is necessarily a cause for verbal cognition in general. This is because such comprehension does not arise when there is doubt or a negative certainty regarding that [intended meaning]. It is precisely the certainty of that [meaning] which [is required].
When multiple word-meanings are presented simultaneously, because there must be a factor of determination (*vinigamaka*) for the connection with only one meaning,

and because it is that which necessitates the assumption of secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*) cannot occur in every case of secondary signification;
thus, in all instances, the sentence-meaning is established solely through the delimitation of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*).

Even though the word (śabda) brings about an experience distinct from perception and inference, it is a restatement (*anuvādaka*) because it apprehends what has already been grasped; thus, only scriptural and Vedic sentences are authoritative (*pramāṇa*).
Some maintain that worldly [words] are merely restatements in this regard.

Even though worldly speech lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) defined as being the instrument for the apprehension of an unknown object, it is nonetheless a means of valid cognition because it possesses the validity characterized by being the instrument for an experience that has that [object] as its form;
thus, it is established that according to the system of the Gurus, there are five types of means of valid cognition.

For the Bhāṭṭas, there are six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), consisting of the five means of valid cognition taught by the Guru (Prabhākara) together with non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*abhāvapramāṇa*). For the Paurāṇikas,
there are six means of valid cognition according to the Vedānta doctrine, augmented by the two means of valid cognition of probability (*saṃbhava*) and tradition (*aitihya*).
Immediately after the eight means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), having thus defined the divisions of the means of valid cognition, the four categories of objects (*padārtha*) are now defined.
This is the *Padārthaviveka*.
Now, there are four categories of objects: the ultimate (pāramārthika), the empirical (vyāvahārika), the apparent (prātibhāsika), and the non-existent (tuccha).
Among these, the pure consciousness of Śiva alone is the ultimate; the entire phenomenal world, beginning with the ether, is the empirical.

The four categories of objects have been defined: illusory objects such as a rope-snake, mother-of-pearl-silver, and the mirage in a desert; non-existent objects such as the son of a barren woman and the horn of a hare; and the void (tuccha).

Now, two categories—the seer and the seen—are being defined. Among these, he establishes the absence of the threefold difference in the Supreme Brahman, which is the nature of the Seer. The Seer is consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Some [hold that] consciousness delimited by ignorance is the "seer" (dṛk), according to the venerable teacher Vācaspati Miśra;
[while] consciousness reflected in ignorance is [the seer], according to the venerable teachers of the Vivaraṇa.

According to the view of the venerable teacher Saṃkṣepaśārīraka, the individual soul (jīva) is consciousness reflected in ignorance (avidyā), while Brahman is consciousness reflected in Māyā. In the view of the teachers of the Vivaraṇa school, there is a plurality of souls due to the plurality of ignorances, whereas in their view, because Māyā is one, it possesses the form of the original prototype (bimba).

Consciousness (caitanya) is the form of the reflection of Brahman; thus, the individual soul (jīva) is one. This is because in the passage, "The wise man crosses over the widespread ignorance," the oneness of ignorance is heard. However, by the statement, "By means of his māyās, Indra becomes many," it follows that there are many individual souls delimited by those respective [māyās].

The establishment of the nature of the seer and the seen is as follows: the "seer" (dṛṣṭi) is consciousness reflected in a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti); the "seen," however, is that which falls within the range of consciousness. Consciousness is the subject (viṣayin), while the entire collection of objects that fall within the range of consciousness in its aspect as the seer constitutes the object (viṣaya).

Some teachers maintain that the consciousness reflected in *avidyā* characterized by *sattva* is the Lord (*īśvara*), while the consciousness reflected in *avidyā* characterized by *tamas* is the individual soul (*jīva*). [They assert] that there are two categories of objects: the Seer (*dṛk*) and the seen (*dṛśya*). But is it not the case that the Seer is also an object of seeing?
Therefore, one must say that there is only one category of object. To this, we reply: no.
Although the object of vision (*dṛśya*) is the object of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the crest of the scriptures, it is not the object of pure consciousness (*caitanya*);
whereas that which is to be known by consciousness is the object of consciousness.
Pure consciousness, being self-luminous, is not an object [of cognition]; therefore, there is no inconsistency regarding the distinction [between the two].

The three types of distinctions— distinctions internal to itself (*svagatabheda*), distinctions from its own kind (*svajātīyabheda*), and distinctions from other kinds (*vijātīyabheda*)— are to be negated. If one asks what the illustration for these is, it is said that in the world, the differentiation of a single tree into leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth is called "internal distinction," while the difference from another tree is [an example of] "distinction from its own kind."
In a tree, there exists a difference from its own kind (sajātīya-bheda), such as the difference from a stone or similar objects which serves as its counter-correlate;
this is a difference from a different kind (vijātīya-bheda). This concludes the refutation of difference.

Immediately following this, by the statement that "just as the sky of Brahman, whose nature is existence, is partless, there is no other reality within reality," it is shown that in Brahman there is neither internal differentiation (*svagatabheda*) nor differentiation from its own kind (*sajātīyabheda*).
While the *māyā* which is the cause of the world and its effects exist, there is no differentiation of those [phenomena] within the real Brahman.

If it is asked how this is so: just as in the world there is no difference in the painting-potency of a painter, so too there is no distinction between the potency of *māyā* and the Brahman that is pure existence (*sanmātra*); thus it is established that for Brahman there is no difference of a different class (*vijātīya-bheda*). Even if such a difference exists, it is false (*mithyābhūta*) and therefore not real.

The scriptural statement of the final conclusion regarding this matter is as follows: "Brahman is indeed one without a second; for in that [Brahman], there is no plurality," according to the meaning of the scriptural passage.

It is established that, through the presence of these three meanings— namely, the affirmation of oneness in the three words "one only, non-dual," the determination of unity, and the negation of duality— it is proven by scripture that Brahman is, respectively, devoid of the threefold distinctions of internal, homogeneous, and heterogeneous difference.
The discrimination of superimposition (*adhyāropa-viveka*):
Immediately following this, there are superimposition and negation (*apavāda*), which constitute the two-fold conceptual construction;
these are like the mental fabrication of a snake, silver, or a thief where none exist, upon objects such as a rope, mother-of-pearl, or a post that do actually exist.
The superimposition (adhyāsa) consists in the conceptualization of māyā and other such things, which do not exist in Brahman whose nature is reality; thus, there is an attribution (adhyāropa).

The discrimination by way of negation (*apavādaviveka*) follows immediately after: just as "that which was a snake is a rope," "that which was silver is mother-of-pearl," or "that which was a thief is a post," so too, through the method of inquiry, the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is unreal, while Brahman alone is real.
The negation [of duality] is that Brahman is the cause of the birth, subsistence, and dissolution of the world through the presence of Māyā.

The Differentiation of the Characteristics of Brahman: Immediately following this, there are three means for the direct realization of the Reality whose nature is pure consciousness—namely, the negative definition (*vyāvṛtti-lakṣaṇa*), the incidental definition (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*), and the essential definition (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*). Among these:

By negating the group of non-self entities—such as the body, mind, vital breath, and senses—with the words "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), that which remains is the Self, which is revealed precisely through the characteristic of the exclusion of those [non-self things].
