What is this so-called "exclusion of the other"? It is the distinction between that Brahman and the body and so forth, even though that distinction is of a false nature.

Just as a mistaken mark of fire, such as [smoke], is an indicator of fire, so too this [scriptural statement] is an indicator of Brahman. For instance, in the statement "The moon is at the tip of the branch," the fact that the moon—which does not actually reside at the tip of the branch—is described as being there serves as an indicator. Similarly, the Self is indicated by its being the cause of the world, which consists of beings such as Bhūtas that do not reside within the Self.

That which is made known is the extrinsic definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*); for example, in the case of "the sun is supreme light," the supreme light—which is distinct from us—serves as the indicator of the sun.
In contrast, truth, knowledge, bliss, and so forth, which indicate the very nature of the Self, are the intrinsic definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*).

Through the knowledge of the mutual non-difference between the categories of reality, consciousness, bliss, and so forth, Brahman is understood as that which is distinct from reality, consciousness, and bliss.

The Discrimination of the Five Characteristics follows immediately after. The fivefold category of reality—consisting of existence, consciousness, bliss, eternity, and perfection—is the defining characteristic (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) of the Self; for when that [Self] is unknown, as in such expressions as "I did not know," and so forth...

That which exists at all times and in all states, such as waking and others, without being subject to sublation, even when the functions of desire and so forth are manifest or unmanifest, is the nature of Being (*sadrūpa*). Existence (*satva*) is the state of being unsublated throughout the three periods of time.
That which is the counter-positive of a negation across the three times is false (*mithyā*); that which is not its counter-positive is true (*satya*). [For example: "This is silver."
If it is asked, "Since things such as shell-silver, which are perceived as being sublated by the cognition 'this is not silver' following an error,
are false, how can the world be false given the absence of any such perception of its sublation?"—
the answer is that here, within Brahman, the world is sublated by such scriptural texts as "Not this, not this" (neti neti).

Because phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is false, the Brahman distinct from it is real; it is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) whose nature is illumination regarding the objects consisting of ignorance superimposed upon its own self, along with its effects and their dependencies in all states.
And that consciousness, which does not cease to exist throughout the three periods of time, is never such that it "does not exist" or "is not illumined."

That which is fit for conventional usage is the state of being the object of supreme love, which is the very nature of bliss; and that Self, whose form is consciousness, has bliss as its inherent nature because it is the locus of supreme love. Whatever is not thus is not thus, like suffering, which is never found to be so.
"Of an eternal nature" means devoid of cessation— that is, the result is that it is free from destruction;
"perfection" consists in its connection with all empirical and illusory objects by virtue of being the accomplisher of all goals.
Regarding the consideration of bliss (*ānanda-vicāra*):

immediately following this, the Self (*ātman*) is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*). In all states, there ought to be a manifestation of the nature of bliss just as there is of the nature of existence and consciousness; yet that [manifestation] does not exist, and thus [the Self is considered].

How is it that its nature is bliss? To this it is said: the light of a lamp, which consists of both heat and illumination, exists pervading the house; however, there is no pervasion of the heat [in the same way]. In water, the sensation of heat becomes manifest, but the manifestation of the light does not.

Just as the existence of the qualities of heat-touch and luminous form is manifested in wood, so too the existence of stones and other such things is manifested; likewise, the existence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda) is manifested in the intellect when it is in a state of delusion consisting of ignorance through the quality of tamas, and in a state of passion through the quality of rajas.

In the state of intense activity (*ghoravṛtti*) consisting of passion (*rāga*), without the manifestation of both *sattva* and *cit*, the manifestation of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*) is not possible; whereas in the state of tranquility (*śāntavṛtti*) consisting of detachment (*vairāgya*) through the quality of purity (*sattvaguṇa*), there is the manifestation of the triad of the natures of *sattva*, *cit*, and *ānanda*.
By the statement "there is throbbing," he becomes one whose nature is the self of bliss.

Following the analysis of the nature of existence (*sattāsvarūpaviveka*), [the author] next explains, in sequence, the distinction between the limiting adjuncts (*upādhibheda*) of the five natures. How so?
There are three types of existence: empirical existence (*vyāvahārikasattā*), apparent existence (*prātibhāsikasattā*), and ultimate existence (*pāramārthikasattā*). Among these—

If the existence of jars and other objects, though unknown during states such as deep sleep and fainting until the attainment of disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya), becomes manifest again upon waking just as before, that is empirical existence (sāvyāvahārikasattā). Pa. ||
And because it is differentiated from consciousness by the defect of ignorance, the object of perception is distinct from consciousness.
It is established in the treatises that it possesses conventional existence.

The very existence of objects such as nacre-silver, dream-objects, and the like—which are non-existent after waking, even though they were experienced at the time of perception—is their "apparent existence" (*prātibhāsika-sattā*).
That which exists only for the duration of its perception and is insentient is "apparent" (*prātibhāsika*). It is produced by defects other than [the root] ignorance (*ajñāna*).
The ultimate reality is the very existence of Brahman, which is the substratum of all conceptualization and is characterized by invisibility and non-dissolution.

Furthermore, due to the difference in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), there are four kinds of consciousness among the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), the immutable witness (*kūṭastha*), and Brahman; [these are] those which [are reflected] in the water of a jar...

The sky with clouds, stars, and lightning; the objective sky reflected in the water of clouds, dew, and frost; and the space delimited by a jar within the great space—these are the fourfold illustrations in sequence.
The distinction of the adjuncts of bliss; bliss is of eight kinds. [Verse]
The bliss of sense objects is the first; the bliss of Brahman is beyond that.
This very bliss of latent impressions (vāsanā) is likewise the primary bliss.
Nijānanda, Mahānanda, Advaitasukhātmaka,
and Vidyānanda— these eight are proclaimed and renowned in the Vedas.
Among these, when there is the attainment of objects such as women and the like, the bliss that is perceived is the bliss of sense-objects (*viṣayānanda*).
The bliss experienced at the time of deep sleep is the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*).
[Objection: But since there is an absence of the functioning of the senses and the mind during deep sleep, how can there be an experience of the bliss of Brahman? How so?

Listen: regarding the memory upon waking from deep sleep, "I slept happily; I was not aware of anything," there is no lack of experience, nor is there any lack of justification for that memory. This is because, even in the absence of an experience characterized by a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there exists an experience in the form of the Witness (*sākṣin*) qualified by a modification of ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, at the moment of emerging from sleep, neither the experience nor the memory is untenable.

The bliss of recollection (*smaryamāṇānanda*) is the bliss of latent impressions (*vāsanānanda*). The bliss perceived when there is a state of equanimity (*upekṣābuddhi*), free from the duality of rejection and acquisition, is the primary bliss (*mukhyānanda*). When the mind dissolves through the practice of yoga, the bliss that manifests is innate bliss (*nijānanda*), which exists amidst objects such as beloved women and the like.
When it is revealed that he is his own dearest beloved, the bliss that manifests is designated as *ātmananda* (the bliss of the Self).
When there is the discernment that the phenomenal world of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-prapañca*) is illusory and that only the realization of one's true nature is real,
the bliss that is perceived is *advaitānanda* (non-dual bliss), which is the unity of the individual soul and Brahman (*jīva-brahmaikya*).
The bliss experienced when the immediate knowledge arising from the great sentences (mahāvākya) that convey [the truth] is being realized is called the bliss of knowledge (vidyānanda).

The discrimination of non-existence (*abhāvaviveka*) refers to the four types of non-existence— namely, prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)— which, when mentioned, are not connected to the eternal state of Brahman; among these [four],...

Prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is the absence of the counter-positive and the producer prior to the production of an object, such as a jar, in its material causes like clay; it is the absence perceived in such cognitions as "a jar will exist here in these potsherds. Destruction non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is the absence produced by a counter-positive such as the striking of a hammer.

The absolute negation (*atyantābhāva*) is precisely the absence whose counter-positive is superimposed upon a locus through the relation of inherence, as in "there is no flower in the sky. Mutual negation (*anyonyābhāva*) is the absence whose counter-positiveness is delimited by the relation of identity, as is cognized in such perceptions as "a jar is not a cloth" and "a cloth is not a jar."

The logicians (Tārkika) and others maintain that it [the absence] is eternal; whereas the Vedāntins hold that it has the same ontological status as its counter-positive, which is perceived as distinct from its material cause (upādāna), while in the case of the material cause, it is of the very nature of the locus itself— at the time of the counter-positive, it exists together with its material cause.
Furthermore, because that which is being perceived cannot possibly be non-separate from itself.

The three types of limitation are limitation by time, limitation by space, and limitation by substance. These three are to be negated in the state of the fullness of Brahman; among them, [limitation by time] is the state of being perceived as "not existing" at a particular time.

Delimitation by time (*kālapariccheda*): being perceived as existing in one place and not existing in another place is delimitation by space (*deśapariccheda*). Being perceived as "this object exists" and "this object does not exist" is delimitation by substance (*vastupariccheda*). [Everything] is "existent" (*sat*) because it has attained identity with existence (*sattātādātmyāpannatayā*).
Brahman, which is existence, appears as everything in the form of the threefold delimitation.
Regarding the distinction of names such as "jīva" and so forth:

immediately following this, it was asked how the conceptualization of the conventional usage of names and so on for the fourfold group—jīva, īśvara, and the rest—which are distinct from the previously mentioned difference in the nature of consciousness, occurs in sequence. First, there is the *jīva*.

It is threefold, consisting of the forms of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña. Among these, the one who identifies with the individual gross body is the Vyāvahārika-jīva (empirical individual soul). "The consciousness reflected in the intellect is the primary meaning of the term 'Thou' (tvaṃ-pada)," and so forth—these are synonyms for Viśva. Following that is the one who identifies with the individual subtle body.

The "apparent individual soul" (*prātibhāsika-jīva*) is imagined in the dream state; these are synonyms for the *taijasa*. Following that, the one who identifies with the individual causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra-vyaṣṭy-abhimānin*), characterized by the limiting adjunct of the effect (*kāryopādhi*) conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopahita*), and identifying with the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti-avasthā-abhimānin*); these are synonyms for the *prājña*.
There are three selves— the individual self (jīvātman), the inner self (antarātman), and the supreme self (paramātman). Among these, the individual self is that which, like a red-hot iron ball,
possesses all the transactions of worldly existence through its relationship as the owner of the body and so forth.
Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, the individual soul (jīva) experiences neither the attainment nor the non-attainment of saṃsāra;
that inner self (antarātman) is the Supreme Self (paramātman), who, like the sun, is the witness of the worldly dealings of the individual soul and the inner self.
The persistence of modification is like the movement of the sun in water; like the moon seen running in a cloud moving across the sky;
like the movement of trees on a bank when a boat travels down a river; and like the sunlight reaching through a window.

Just as the movement of sunlight [is perceived] through the movement of the hand, one should understand that the two states of birth and death belong to the body; for the self, which is changeless like the [sun], there is the worldly transaction of saṃsāra only when it has attained the state of a living being (jīva) through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body.
Furthermore, the differentiation of the names of the Lord (Īśvara) exists as threefold: Virāṭ Puruṣa, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Antaryāmin.
Among these, those such as Vaiśvānara—the one who identifies with the aggregate of gross bodies—belong to Virāṭ Puruṣa.

Synonyms: Immediately following, "the one who identifies with the aggregate of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra)," "the thread-soul (sūtrātman)," and so forth, are synonyms for Hiraṇyagarbha; [he who identifies with the aggregate of the causal body (kāraṇaśarīra) is...]"

The Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) is designated by such terms as: the Consciousness conditioned by ignorance (ajñānopahita-caitanya), that which has the causal adjunct (kāraṇopādhika), that which has Māyā as its adjunct (māyopādhika), the manifestation of Māyā (māyābhāsa), the wielder of Māyā (māyāvī), the source of the universe (jagadyoni), consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), the Imperishable (akṣara), the Unmanifest (avyakta), the Undifferentiated (avyākṛta), the variegated Brahman (śabalabrahma), the Brahman with attributes (saguṇabrahma), the Supreme (parama), the Supreme Deity (paradevatā), and the primary referent of the word "That" (tatpadamukhyārtha). These and others refer to the Inner Ruler.
Synonyms.
Furthermore, regarding the analogy of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*): when it is asked what example there is for the threefold nature of the Lord,
the answer is that it is like a single cloth that is washed by itself, without being connected to any other variegated cloth or substance.

It is so designated. Just as [an object] is said to be fashioned by an application of barley-gruel paste on top, or said to be marked with a blue form, or said to be colored by filling it with appropriate colors on top; in that very same way, the Supreme Brahman, when initially devoid of *māyā* and its effects, is called Consciousness (*cit*). Thereafter—
Through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *māyā*, which serves as the cause of all, it is designated by the term "Inner Controller" (*antaryāmin*). Furthermore,

through the limiting adjunct of the collective subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra-samaṣṭi*), which is the effect of the unmanifest and unquintuplicated elements (*avyakta-apañcīkṛta-bhūta-kārya*), it is called the "Thread-Self" (*sūtrātman*).
Above that, by means of the adjunct consisting of the collective gross body— which is the effect of the fivefold-compounded unmanifest elements—
he is called Virāj.
The Concordance of Examples:

Immediately following this, the example of a painted canvas was stated regarding Brahman. When it is asked what those paintings are, [the answer is: sentient beings beginning with Viriñci (Brahmā) and ending with insects, as well as insentient objects such as mountains, rivers, and so forth.
Thus, the entire world, consisting of both the insentient and the sentient, becomes like the illustration of a painting.

Furthermore, regarding the conceptualization of qualities and so forth: when it is asked how the world— consisting of many sentient and insentient entities that are illusory in nature— appears within Brahman, which is the ultimate reality whose nature is consciousness, it is as follows:
If the paintings of humans and so forth,

as well as garments and ornaments endowed with various colors yet incapable of warding off cold and the like, exist as being similar to a real supporting cloth that is uniform in form and capable of warding off cold and the like; [then they would be real].

In that painting, the mountains, rivers, and other features exist without being properly integrated with the canvas that serves as their support. Likewise, within the Brahman whose nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), the empirical individual souls (*jīvas*), though appearing as distinct entities, are indeed endowed with the same nature as consciousness; they are but reflections of consciousness (*cid-ābhāsa-cetanās*).

[They] become so; by this it was determined that all the world, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious—such as clay and other insentient forms which lack equality with consciousness—is superimposed upon Brahman, whose nature is consciousness. Immediately thereafter...

Omniscience, universal sovereignty, universal controllership, universal inner rulership, being the self of all, and omnipotence—these alone are the primary attributes of the Lord. The capacity to act, to refrain from acting, and to act otherwise constitutes the threefold power of the Lord, which is called His majesty. Immediately thereafter—
Creation, maintenance, dissolution, control, and entrance are the fivefold functions of the Lord.

Immediately following the illustration of the Lord's activity, it was asked: "How is the agency of many acts, such as creation and so forth, possible in the Lord, whose nature is the changeless, non-dual Brahman? To this it was replied: "Just as the sun, without desire, effort, or the like..."

Spreading water in the form of rain by means of his own annual rays, he himself enters into that water in the form of a reflection; having caused the reflections of water in the clouds and so forth to vanish,
and having established the reflection of water by means of the moonlight and other rays, he drinks the water with his hot rays.

Just as [the individual soul] subsequently unifies the reflection with itself, so too Maheśvara— having become the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) through the predominance of consciousness (*cit*) by means of His own power of *māyā*, and being called the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) through the predominance of the insentient (*jaḍa*)— creates the effects such as the intellect (*buddhi*).

Having entered into this body and so forth in the form of the individual soul (jīva), he is said to be the experiencer of karmas; then, by means of his power of governance, he governs both the objects of experience and the experiencer. [Verse:
His body, which has come into being through Māyā, consists of the quality of sattva and the quality of tamas.
He alone, and no other, shall be that Rudra for the dissolution of the three forms.

Salutations to you, whose nature is Rudra, who are endowed with both existence and non-existence, whose self is characterized by darkness during the dissolution of the universe, and whose body is composed of pure knowledge.

By this collection of Purāṇic statements, it becomes easy to distinguish between the collective and the individual: having first withdrawn the multitude of effects by means of the form of Rudra as described therein, He subsequently exists in the form of the Śruti and the Teacher, unifying the individual souls with Himself.
Both the aggregate (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).

Just as one understands a forest to be a single entity composed of many trees, the individual soul’s conceit that "all [trees] are of the nature of my own self" constitutes its aggregate form as the Lord. Within that very same forest, there is the notion: "This is one tree; this is another... [and so on].
Just as there are distinct instruments for each individual tree, so too the individual's identification with various separate bodies constitutes its state as a *vyaṣṭi* (individual manifestation).

Furthermore, the non-discrimination of names such as the Immutable (Kūṭastha) and so forth refers to the consciousness that is the substratum of the triad of individual souls beginning with Viśva; this is the Fourth (Turya), the meaning of the word "Self" (Svayam),
the witness, the ultimate reality of the soul, the inner self (Pratyagātman), the inner ruler (Antaryāmī), and the synthesizer (Anusaṃdhātā).
The limited individual soul (avacchinna-jīva), the referent of the word "thou" (tvaṃ-padalakṣyārtha),
and so forth, are synonyms for the immutable witness (kūṭastha).

Furthermore, the names synonymous with Brahman— such as Antaryāmin (the Inner Ruler), Īśvara-traya-adhiṣṭhātā (the Presiding Lord of the three Lords), Parabrahman (the Supreme Brahman), Paratattva (the Supreme Reality), Paramātman (the Supreme Self),
Sarvādhiṣṭhātā (the Universal Presider), Viśuddhacit (Pure Consciousness), and Tatpadalakṣyārtha (the referent of the word "That")— belong to Brahman.
Synonyms:
*Dṛgvivekasāra*.
Immediately thereafter: "Just as clay alone, through name and form, becomes manifold such as jars and the like..."

Just as gold, though being one alone, appears in the form of all ornaments such as bracelets and crowns through a mere verbal designation (*vācārambhaṇa*); just as water, though being one alone, appears in the form of a collection of foam, waves, and so forth by the power of the wind; just as a single lamp appears manifold through the apertures of jars; and just as the wind, though being one alone...

Just as a single sound, produced by the vocal cords of a singer, becomes manifold in the form of various melodies (*rāga*) through its differentiation into sweet, deep, and other qualities according to the holes of the flute; just as the sky, though one, appears in many ways through the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as houses and the like; and just as a single resonance becomes multiform through the variety of musical instruments—so it is with this [consciousness].

Just as the sky is one, yet appears variegated with elephants, horses, and so forth within the segments of a plantain leaf; just as the moon and the sun, though each is singular, attain multiplicity through [reflections in] water-jars and the like; and just as the face, though single, [appears differently] due to the diversity of mirrors.
Just as the single number "one" becomes the numbers "hundred" and "thousand" through many dots,

so too, within the one Consciousness, the previously mentioned conventional distinctions of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), and so forth, are logically established by the conceptualization of limiting adjuncts (upādhi); all such matters are explained in the *Dṛgviveka*.
The Discrimination of the Nature of Māyā: Subsequently, just as the stain of the moon, though beginningless, reaches the moon and,
without obscuring the moon, appears as if being illuminated by it, so too is primordial ignorance (anādibhūtam ajñānam).
In the worldly convention expressed as "I do not know myself," although the self is reached by the self and is known by the self without being concealed, it remains [unrecognized]. [Verse]
Furthermore, just as the burning power of fire, though obstructed by the application of a magnet or similar means, is not distinct from the fire and does not abandon it; so too is the case here.
Just as [the sphoṭa], though not manifest, is understood through its effects such as the sphoṭa itself; so it is here.
Distinct from Brahman, it cannot, apart from Brahman, possess characteristics such as luminosity and so forth.

Although it is inferable from its effects such as space (*viyat*) and so forth, the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*)— which takes the form of the visible world— is capable of bringing about the impossible and serves as the cause of all misfortune;
this is the definition of *māyā*.

The five characteristics of *māyā* are unreality (*asat*), insentience (*jaḍa*), suffering (*duḥkha*), impermanence (*anityatva*), and fragmentariness (*khaṇḍitatva*). Among these, that which is unreal is like the horn of a hare; that which is insentient is like stone and the like;
and that which is of the nature of suffering consists of the terrible and deluded mental states of a consciousness composed of *rajas* and *tamas*, namely, the world of objects (*dṛśya*).

The body and so forth, which are the counter-correlates of cessation, are impermanent in nature, limited by time, and fragmented in their very essence. This [worldly state] is unreal, unattainable, and takes the form of manifold sufferings;
likewise, that other [state] is impermanent and consists of fragmentation due to the passage of time.
Furthermore, the ninefold manner in which Māyā is indefinable is as follows:

it is different, non-different, and consisting of both; it is associated with the category of existence (sat), its nature is cessation (nivṛtti), it is real, it possesses a body composed of both [existence and non-existence], and it is both partless and possessed of parts—thus is Māyā indefinable.
There are nine types [of cognition]. Among these, the distinct cognitions of jars and so forth are diverse;

however, the cognition of the oneness of a jar as a jar is non-different. Even though the parts, such as hair and nails, appear individually within the body, they are all indeed of the nature of the body.

Even those things belonging to the body, which serves as the instrument for enjoyment, appear as non-adherent; thus, that which is perceived as distinct or non-distinct exists, while that which is perceived as non-existent—such as the sky-flower—is non-existent. That which possesses form is indeed possessed of parts, though it is conventionally designated as "formless."
The ignorance that [conceives] non-existence, the partless, and Mount Meru as being inexpressible does not consist of both the partless and the possessed-of-parts.
Illusion consists of the threefold cognition that follows immediately thereafter, namely,
the cognition consisting of the knowledge of the connection with scripture, the knowledge of the connection with reasoning, and the knowledge of the connection with the world.
Having pursued [the inquiry] with speed, it is stated that [the world] is as void as a sky-flower,
as indescribable as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and as eternal as the Self.
Furthermore, the "fivefold māyā" consists of *tamas*, *māyā*, *moha*, *avidyā*, and *anṛta*; thus it is called the fivefold māyā.
Among these, *tamas* is so designated because it obscures the bliss that is non-different from the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīva*).
By the phrase "the cause of the world appearing in a form other than [its true nature]," it is called *māyā*.
Because it produces erroneous cognitions—such as that of silver in mother-of-pearl—with respect to the world as it appears, it is called *moha*.
It is called "ignorance" (avidyā) because it is being destroyed by the knowledge consisting of the understanding of the meaning of sentences produced by the scriptures;
it is called "unreal" (anṛta) because it is other than that which has the nature of existence (sadrūpa).
The two properties of Māyā immediately following are contraction and expansion; these are indeed the two properties of Māyā.
Just as a painted canvas, by its unfolding, displays various images and, by its contraction, conceals those images, so it is here.
Māyā, by means of its nature of expansion, manifests the phenomenal world (jagat-prapañca), and by means of its nature of contraction, it causes that phenomenal world to dissolve.
This is the twofold quality of māyā.

Immediately following this, there are two attributes of Māyā: non-independence (*asvatantratā*) and independence (*svatantratā*). Among these, because Māyā is false—consisting in being the counter-positive of a negation at all three times—it does not appear apart from the Reality that is Consciousness; this is called non-independence. [As stated in] the verse:
For the self has non-attachment as its intrinsic nature, due to the reason known as being partless.
And by the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas, it is declared that Brahmā attained union [with her].
This [self] is neither an agent nor an enjoyer, because its status as the substratum of knowledge is lost;
for its existence [as such] is not possible through cognitions such as "knowledge is in me."
Because Brahman is sublated by Vedic knowledge and because it teaches difference.
How can there be the knowledge "I am the enjoyer" within the eternal Self?
In the cognition of "I," both suffering and happiness manifest.
Suffering is to be understood as belonging to the mind, while happiness likewise belongs to the self.

The state of independence (*svatantratā*) is that which, by repeatedly superimposing agency and other attributes— which reside in the intellect— upon the Self, makes the Self, which is the witness of all and devoid of attachment, appear as consisting of the phenomenal world of the individual soul and so forth.
The Definition of Falsity:
Immediately following that, one might ask: what is this so-called "false"? Is it entirely void, like a flower in the sky? No;
rather, it is something that exists as it is perceived, like an elephant created in a dream.
That which is sublated by the certainty arising from reflection (*vicāra*)— such as that derived from scripture (*śruti*) and so forth— is false (*mithyā*). Furthermore,
"false" means either that which coexists with its own absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) as delimited by ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*),
or that which is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence residing in a locus different from its own locus.

Alternatively, the collection of phenomena perceived during the waking state is false, because it possesses the counter-correlativity of a cessation that is co-extensive with non-selfhood; it is false because it is an object of perception, like the collection of phenomena consisting of elephants, horses, and so forth imagined in a dream. Nor is this [the case].
It should not be argued that the elephants, horses, and so forth seen in a dream are real because they are perceived during that state, just like the phenomenal world perceived in the waking state;
for if the dream-world were real, then after the scripture teaches the creation of chariots and other things within the dream, it would subsequently state that they do not exist there.
Because [the claim that] "chariots and so forth" would contradict the cognition of sublation.
Furthermore, the three functions of *māyā* are as follows: *māyā*, which is of the nature of pure *sattva*; *avidyā*, which is of the nature of impure *sattva*;
and *prakṛti*, which is of the nature of *tamas*-predominance; these are the three functions of *māyā*. Among them—
Māyā itself, having remained as if unified with the Supreme Brahman during deep sleep and dissolution,

and having dwelt within dream and waking states, attains a state of differentiation; when reflected upon the Brahman-consciousness, it is called the Lord (Īśvara), whose nature consists of consciousness qualified by attributes such as omniscience.
When it is said that "the existent is the object of practice," it follows that the existent becomes the impeller;
by this it is stated that Māyā alone, having become the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the Lord,
acts as the deluder, and furthermore, it is precisely ignorance (avidyā) appearing in manifold forms.
Having become the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the individual souls (*jīvas*), who constitute the category of bound beings (*paśu*) characterized as enjoyers, [Prakṛti] exists deluding them.
Furthermore, Prakṛti itself, being of the nature of the object of enjoyment, is called the category of the bond (*pāśa*);
remaining in a state of equilibrium of the three qualities (*guṇatrayasamānāvasthā*), it subsequently [enters] into ignorance (*avidyā*).
For the sake of the experience of the individual souls reflected therein,
and for the sake of accomplishing all effects, she remains manifesting and fashioning the phenomenal world through the mere act of appearing in the presence of the Lord.
The sequence of creation beginning with the Mahat:

Primordial Nature (prakṛti) itself first attains the principle of time (kālatattva), and subsequently, undergoing transformation under the influence of that time, it is called the principle of Mahat. Immediately thereafter, the principle of Mahat also...
Even when provided with water-sprinkling, [the seed] does not reach the state of a sprout but remains as before; like a seed that has reached the state of an *udbhijja* (germinating plant),
there exists a false cognition distinct from the cause and distinct from the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) which has become a non-cause.
In its non-conceptual (nirvikalpa) form, it is called the state of falsity. Furthermore, having attained a differentiation of qualities through the principle of Mahat,
it is called the root-ahaṃkāra, which is described as the primary superimposition (adhyāsa) that acts as the semblance of the non-conceptual nature of false knowledge.
It comes to be.

Immediately thereafter, the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are indeed illumination (prakāśa), activity (pravṛtti), and delusion (moha), which constitute the forms of the qualities such as sattva; these are synonymous names for the qualities of sattva and so forth, namely vaikārika, taijasa, and bhūtādi.
Among these, by means of the quality of sattva...

From the *mānasa* (mind) arises the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-catuṣṭaya*), and from the quality of *rajas* arise the five sense organs (*jñānendriya*) beginning with the ear, as well as the five organs of action (*karmendriya*) beginning with speech and the five vital airs (*prāṇa*) beginning with *prāṇa*.
From the quality of *tamas* arises the fivefold gross elements (*bhūta-pañcaka*) beginning with space (*ākāśa*).
Immediately after the fourfold internal organs, through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) and the integration of the elements,
objects such as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), the worlds (*bhuvana*), bodies (*śarīra*), and jars (*ghaṭa*) arise. Immediately thereafter—
The functions of the internal organs, beginning with the mind (*manas*), are respectively: reflection (*cintana*), determination (*niścaya*), egoism (*abhimāna*), and discernment (*avadhāraṇa*).

Their presiding deities (*adhidevatās*) are Candra (the Moon), Caturmukha (Brahmā), Kṣetrajña (the Knower of the Field), and Tripurāntaka (Śiva). These reside in the sphere of the heart (*hṛdayagolaka*).
It becomes a basis.

Furthermore, regarding the pentad of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*): the sequential functions of the organs of knowledge, beginning with the ear, consist of the operations of hearing, touching, seeing, tasting, and smelling with respect to their respective objects,
such as sound and the rest.
The directional deities—Dik, Marut, Mitra, Varuṇa, and the Aśvins—are the presiding deities (adhidevatās). The locations are the spheres of the ears and so forth.

Subsequently, just as there is the manifestation of external objects such as sound through the sense organs like hearing, when the ear-cavity is covered by a finger, [the perception of external sound ceases].

The perception of sound existing within the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*), and so forth; the perception of the form of internal darkness when the eyes are closed; and the perception of the sensations of heat and cold upon the intake of food and drink, as well as during belching and other such occurrences.
Since there is the apprehension of objects such as taste, smell, touch, and sound— which constitute distinct forms of perception— that establishes the existence of the five organs of action;
these are the organs of action, beginning with speech.
They perform the functions characterized by speaking, taking, going, releasing, and experiencing pleasure.

The presiding deities of the lords of creatures (Prajāpatis), who are the creators of the multitude of living beings throughout the three worlds, who are the fearsome death for all worlds like the sun that destroys the enemies of Vaiśvānara’s jaws, shine resplendent within the spheres of the mouth and other [senses].

The discrimination regarding the internal and so forth follows immediately after. Among those, the fourteen types consisting of the fourfold internal organs, the organs of knowledge, and the organs of action are the *ādhyātmika* (internal). Their objects are the *ādhibhautika* (pertaining to beings).
Their presiding deities are called the *ādhidaivika* (pertaining to the divine).

Furthermore, the conjunction with the roots of the sense organs consists precisely of the presiding deities of those organs. The sense organs of the Virāṭ Puruṣa are themselves the body of Hiraṇyagarbha, and that very body exists as the covering of the Antaryāmin.
Furthermore, among the five vital airs (prāṇas) and so forth, the prāṇa-vāyu, residing in the region of the heart, performs inhalation and exhalation;
the apāna-vāyu, situated in the region of the anus, expels waste and urine; and the samāna-vāyu resides in the region of the navel.

The udāna-vāyu, situated in the region of the throat, distributes the essence of the food consumed throughout all the limbs and functions by producing eructation. The vyāna-vāyu, residing in all the limbs, maintains the body.
Furthermore, by means of the nāga-vāyu, there occurs the stretching of the limbs, and by the kūrma-vāyu, yawning.

The upward-moving wind (*udgāra*) is produced by the *kṛkara* wind; hunger and thirst by the *devadatta* wind; laughing and speaking by the *dhanañjaya* wind; and sorrow and passion arise from the same. This very *dhanañjaya* wind, after death, remains for five days, causes the body to swell, bursts it open, and having destroyed it, departs.
Furthermore, when the five winds beginning with nāga are said to be the external winds,
they become the causes for the activities of the organs of action (karmendriya) such as speech;
the five winds beginning with prāṇa become the causes for the activities of the organs of cognition (jñānendriya) such as hearing.

Each of these four winds associated with the individual soul— known as Vairambha, Mukhya, Prabhañjana, and Antaryāmin— is the cause of the activity of the fourfold internal organs, beginning with the mind (manas).
A verse is a transformation of the qualities of the elements.
Furthermore, the elements beginning with earth are indeed maintained in a specific sequence.
They provide the space for the phenomena of the array known as the "coagulation" and "maturation."
These are declared to be "activities" (vyāpāra) according to their respective effects.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—

these are known as their presiding deities (adhidevatās), while fragrance and the other [sensory qualities] are remembered as their attributes (guṇas). Furthermore, regarding the attributes of those elements, there is a verse:
In space there should be one quality, but in air there are two qualities.
The three qualities are said to reside in fire; the four qualities reside in water.
The earth possesses five qualities; how many kinds of its divisions are there?
Space has one quality, which is the nature of an echo; air has two qualities, namely sound and a touch that is neither hot nor cold;
fire has three qualities, namely the sound "bubhuk," a hot touch, and a radiant form; and [these are] the qualities of water.
The four qualities known as sound (*gu-gu* etc.), cold touch, luminous white color,
and sweet taste belong to earth; [earth] also possesses the qualities of *guḍa-guḍa* sound, hard touch, variegated colors such as blue, and various tastes such as sweet and sour.
The five qualities known as fragrance and foul odor, having further transformed the five elements through modification into material objects such as jars and the like,
exist in their various high and low forms as all the qualities within the visible phenomenal world.
One should examine and understand that [the self] appears as if touched by states consisting of manifestation and non-manifestation in things such as jars.
The definition of the triad is as follows:

this triad consists of the knower, the object of knowledge, and the act of knowing. Within that [triad], consciousness reflected in the root-ego is the knower, and consciousness reflected in the mental modification is the act of knowing.
Objects consisting of the primary elements and their derivatives, when presided over by consciousness, are called "knowable."
Furthermore, the principles (tattvas) are said to be twenty-four in number; the root ego (mūlāhaṃkāra),
known as the twenty-fifth principle, is indeed merely the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) residing within that ego.
The individual soul (jīva) is the twenty-sixth; the Lord (īśvara), having māyā as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), is the twenty-seventh.
The Lord, delimited by Māyā, is the twenty-eighth.
That very same Kūṭastha, who is the substrate of both that ego (ahaṃkāra) and the individual soul (jīva), constitutes the nineteenth;
Brahman itself, as the presiding controller of both Māyā and Īśvara, becomes the thirtieth;
and Brahman-consciousness (brahmacaitanya) alone, as conditioned by the non-differentiated Māyā, becomes the thirty-first.

The very reality that manifests as the singular essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānandaikarasasphūrti) constitutes the thirty-second principle; furthermore, although the number of principles becomes manifold due to the distinctions among the objects of inquiry, they are all included within the aforementioned principles. Thus.

One should realize that one's own true nature is the eternally liberated Brahman— the consciousness of Parātpara-Śiva, which is characterized by Māyā as mere existence, free from qualities and unattached to the thirty-two principles.

Furthermore, regarding the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), when the effect arises from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there are two types: sequential emanation and simultaneous emanation. Among these, from the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) arises the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*).

From that arises the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya); from the "I-notion," the seven primordial natures (prakṛtis) known as the five subtle elements (tanmātras); from those [subtle elements] arise the five gross elements (bhūtas); and from those five gross elements arises the manifestation of the universe (prapañca), such as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), bodies, jars, and so forth—this very process is called "gradual creation" (kramasṛṣṭi).

The *cūrṇikā* [states]: "Simultaneous creation. Following sequential creation, [the elements arise] at one and the same time from the waveless ocean, which is devoid of contact with wind, birds, and the like, by the power of the wind.

It is called simultaneous creation because, within the Brahman whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, there arise— possessing the common characteristics of manifold origins such as diverse foam, waves, and bubbles— an uninterrupted series of countless millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), which manifest as a primary expansion of various forms.
Both of these types must be accepted as established by scripture.
Furthermore, regarding the analogy of creation: when an effect arises from its material cause (*prakṛti*),
there is a sequential creation immediately following [the cause], by which one attains the nature of Brahman that was previously unmanifested.
When it is asked how the emergence of all effects can occur within insentient *prakṛti* by means of a Lord who is devoid of transformation, [the answer is:
just as fire blazes in a sun-crystal stone by the sun— which is itself devoid of will and effort—
there is no contradiction in the emergence of effects such as the *mahat* and so forth from *prakṛti* by means of Paraśiva, who is likewise devoid of effort and the like.

Immediately following the fourfold conceptualization of effects, there arises here a fourfold emergence of effects known as the commencement of the transformation of the fluctuations (*vṛtti-pariṇāma*) and their manifestation (*vivarta*).
Of these, the state of being a tent (*paṭakuṭī-bhāva*) [is one such effect].
The four examples are, respectively: milk and curd, thread and cloth, and the forms of a rope and a snake.

What is called *pariṇāma* (evolution) is a change into something else that possesses an equal degree of reality (*sattā*); what is called *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) is a change into something else that possesses a different degree of reality.

The examples of false perception (*mithyādṛṣṭānta*) immediately following are: a rope-snake, a post, a thief, a dream, a magician’s trick, a city of the Gandharvas, silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and the blue sky.
The mirage, water, the yellowness of a conch, a hibiscus flower, the redness of a crystal placed near it, the body, and one's own cognition—
these are the collection of examples for the conceptualization of unreal objects based upon real entities.
The refutation of the fault regarding causality:

Immediately following this, it is indeed stated that the conceptualization of false objects arises within the non-dual Self, which is by nature immutable; for it was previously said that such a delusive object is first cognized.
A verse.
She approaches, casting glances that cannot be directly perceived yet cause the arising of a thousand sons from the heart,
her hands adorned with shimmering golden bracelets.
Having seen in a dream this virtuous woman, who repeatedly pours forth the pure moonlight of her smile in every direction, even this ascetic has become desirous of love.
Just as when a certain lord of ascetics experiences a dream of three forms arising from an intense longing for his father—

though perceived at one and the same time— it is said that there is no loss whatsoever; so too, in the Self who is the witness of all, there is no change through the presence or absence of knowledge, nor through the material nature (*prakṛti*) endowed with the three qualities (*guṇatraya*).
The phenomenal world, consisting of the triad of the deluded knower, the delusive cognition, and the object of that delusion which is the knowable— though it is conceptualized within a single moment—
remains stable precisely because it is said that there is no loss whatsoever to that [reality].

Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of the threefold nature of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*): the world of manifestation consisting of ether and so forth, created by the Lord through *māyā*, exists in a single mode as its own essential nature; within that [world], the individual soul (*jīva*)...

Since the object of pleasure, the object of aversion, and the object of indifference exist as threefold— each being merely a form of enjoyment imagined individually by the modifications of the intellect— it is said that among these, women and the like are objects of pleasure,
tigers and the like are objects of aversion, and grass and the like are objects of indifference.
Furthermore, regarding this object, which is imagined by Īśvara as having a single form yet appears in many ways, there exists a manifold variety of forms imagined by individual living beings (jīva).
When asked what the illustration for this is like, it is said to be an object such as a jewel created by Īśvara.

Although existing as a single uniform nature, it subsequently exists as various things— such as jewels and so forth— imagined through the diversity constructed by the intellects of enjoyers, for each respective object,
for the sake of its own producer.

It exists as an object of desire for one who is capable of attaining it; it exists as an object of aversion for one incapable of attaining it; and it exists as an object of indifference for the dispassionate self.
Furthermore, the very nature of an object created by the Lord, existing in a single form, is perceived by the individual soul (*jīva*)...

To manifest that which exists in various forms within it, conjoined with the imagined mode of being an object of enjoyment, there is yet another single illustration; when asked what that is, it is said: the fleshly form of a certain woman born of her father exists as a single uniform appearance, and she belongs to him alone.

Through forms imagined by the intellect of the enjoyer, she herself exists in manifold ways— as "the son" to the father, as "the daughter-in-law" to the husband, as "the mother" to the son, and as "the daughter-in-law" to the husband’s father; yet, relative to herself, she becomes the regulator for those younger than her,
the regulated for those older than her, and the object of veneration for sons and others.
Having become the worshiper of her father and others, having become the half-body of her husband,
having become the one standing in the eastern quarter for those behind her,
having become the one situated in the northern direction for those in the south, and having become the one standing in the west for those situated in the east— she is that very same [one].
Being delimited by space, time, action, and adjuncts (upādhi), it is designated in many ways.
In this manner, although its object is everything, it becomes twofold: that which is created by Īśvara in a single form, and that which is created by the individual soul (jīva) in manifold forms.
The manifestation of the Lord:

in the midst of that, the very manifestation created by the Lord, being free from sublation and having become a means to liberation in the form of the Guru, the scriptures, and so forth, remains in that state even though it is incapable of being abandoned by itself.

The negation of the threefold world-appearance of the individual soul (jīva): Immediately following this, the world-appearance imagined by the individual soul exists as a cause of bondage; it becomes twofold—namely, the scriptural world-appearance and the non-scriptural world-appearance—and can be abandoned by one seeking liberation.

Furthermore, the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) described in the scriptures exists in two forms: the intense and the mild. Among these, inquiry into the Self and Brahman is called the scriptural [expansion], while desire, anger, and so forth are called the intense phenomenal expansion;
and mental constructs such as rajasic actions and the like are called the mild phenomenal expansion.

It is said that among the three kinds of phenomenal worlds (prapañca) imagined by Jīvaka in this manner, the scriptural phenomenal world can be abandoned after the direct realization of the Self through means such as knowledge;
however, the non-scriptural phenomenal world— whether intense or mild— is, by its very nature, an obstacle to the direct realization of the Self.
It must be abandoned even prior to the practice of knowledge. Immediately thereafter, the dualistic manifestation (ubhayaprapañca),

although already abandoned by him following the direct realization of pure Śiva, persists merely as the appearance of the form of the world— just as the fragrance of musk remains in the form of its scent within a casket even after the musk itself has been removed.

Even for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), the mere latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the delusion of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) remains unavoidable until the attainment of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*); thereafter, when even that [impression] has perished, there remains only the state of being eternally full, pure bliss, and the consciousness of the Self alone, which is devoid of the cognition of anything other than itself.

The secret meaning therein is that "nirvāṇa comes to be. In this context, the scriptural elaboration refers to the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) and so forth. Inquiry into Brahman is defined as the investigation of logical reasoning (*nyāya-parīkṣā*) which determines the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the Vedānta passages conducive to the knowledge of Brahman.
Thus it is said: "That which is to be inquired into is the oneness of the two categories of Brahman and the Self, their identity as the Self;
this pair of terms is what is intended for inquiry by the original authors."
Therefore, the Brahman-Self, being "I," is not to be known through an effect as its mark.
The distinction between those two— namely, that "I am not the Lord"—

is to be realized through direct perception itself by means of a source of knowledge other than the Veda; for while the Brahman-Self is to be known through the Vedanta, no other distinction can be an object of knowledge.
By what can the latent impressions, perceived through beginningless differentiation, be awakened?
Unity is the nature of Brahman and the Self when all obstructions have been removed;
for in that state, the worldly relationship of being the knower and the known between the two does not exist at all.
It is held that [the Self] is veiled by the impressions associated with beginningless ignorance;
the destruction of this obscuring [veil], however, occurs through the certainty arising from the teachings of the Vedānta.
Therefore, their identity is to be known through the Vedas alone and not otherwise;
the determination of the first Sūtra constitutes the definition of Brahman as the object to be sought.
The second aphorism intends to establish that "the origin and so forth of this [world] is indeed the defining characteristic [of Brahman].
Now, one might ask: how can the origin and so forth, which reside in something else, be the defining characteristic of Brahman?
Furthermore, tell me: how can the status of being its cause exist in Brahman, who is devoid of attributes?
The defining characteristic of each respective locus should be understood as being like a serpent upon the branch-tip of a garland.
The agency in the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe is the defining characteristic of Brahman.
In the absence of that [agency], there is no defining characteristic in that which possesses it; it is not a characteristic of the essential nature itself.

A false, counterfeit sign may appear similar to that which awakens [to truth], yet one's own true nature is considered to be characterized by the form of reality, knowledge, and bliss. The distinction between reality, knowledge, and bliss, which is established in the world, ceases [to exist as a duality].
The oneness of that [Self] must be known through such statements as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) in order to sublate the cognition of difference;
however, since qualities such as knowledge are already established in the world, they are not to be known through the Śruti.
This logic of the second sūtra is now applied to consider the third:
does the status of being the source (yoni) of the Śāstra exist in Brahman, or does it not?
The author of the treatise always declares thus; otherwise, it would not be a valid means of knowledge.
For if it were of human origin, there would be the possibility of error; thus, a fourth [alternative] is impossible.
Because it is not produced by any cognizable knowledge, there is no contemplation of a flood of defects;
because it lacks the nature of being composed for a specific purpose, it possesses no human authorship.
The *Bhārata* and other such works are considered human compositions because they consist of arrangements made with a specific intent.
Indeed, there exists no means of valid cognition for such a nature in another self;
nor does it exist by virtue of desire, because [Brahman] has already attained all desires.
It is established that Brahman alone is the author of the scripture, on account of its being like a natural breath and so forth.
Because he is the author of the treatise that illuminates everything, he is the supreme omniscient one.

If [Brahman] were established as an already-existent entity like a jar, how could it be known through scripture (*śāstra*), given that scripture is its source and authority? Furthermore, [it would be so] because of the arguments for its being devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*) and because of its being weightless (*laghutva*). Thus, [the opponent argues].
Because it is devoid of form, marks, and so forth, the Supreme Self is not an object of inference;
nor does it possess attributes such as cognition and the like, as asserted by the Naiyāyikas.
It is established that [the Lord] is not [merely] out of respect [for scripture], because He is the manifestation of perfect bliss;
the eternal Brahman is accessible through the Vedas alone, and by virtue of being the source of the scriptures,
that Brahman is perfectly harmonized with the Upanishadic texts in the fourth sūtra.

For the Vedāntas are indeed the enjoiners; otherwise, they would not even possess the nature of scripture. [The Upanishads] establish that the agent and so forth are subordinate to the performance of ritual action, and that the consciousness of the deities is the deity itself, according to scripture.
That the deity is mere sound is the conclusion established by the Mīmāṃsā scriptures.
Whence could Brahmā come, and whence the gods, given the consequence of partiality and other such faults?
And those who always perform actions that are prohibited.
For them, heaven and liberation are said by the wise to be continuous; indeed,
from the performance of prohibited acts comes only the state of hell—
this is the certainty of the Vedas that awaken the understanding of unprecedented realization.
Alternatively, since it is the first object of action, that [world] is understood by them;
however, it is not logical that Brahman alone should be the object of understanding in the Vedas and Vedāntas.
We say that in this regard, it is understood because of its being something previously unknown (*apūrva*).
By means of all the statements of the Vedānta, through such indicative marks as the opening [of the texts] and so forth.
Since it is fruitless and devoid of the effects of cultivation, how can it be realized?
For when Brahman—the pure, attributeless, eternal, and auspicious—is to be fully awakened to, [there is no object of realization].
The cessation of what is harmful is the fruit that arises from the Vedānta.
For when there is a doubt as to whether [the object] is to be understood as an *apūrva* (unseen potency) or as a *bhāvanā* (productive activity),
it is said that the *apūrva* is the thing to be accomplished (*kārya*), because [if it were a *bhāvanā*,] faults such as prolixity (*gaurava*) would follow.
For the sake of brevity, only that which is previously unknown and productive of fruit, as taught by the Veda, [is to be considered].
Thus, the meaning accessible through Vedānta, which is distinct from the meaning of the ritual section (Karmakāṇḍa),
is determined by all the wise as being free from contradiction with the Vedānta and other sources;
for those who prescribe the means of realization are indeed dependent upon Brahman.
Because they are Vedic, all the Vedāntas are indeed injunctions;
and because they enjoin reflection (*manana*) and so forth, we joyfully declare therein that realization is something to be performed,
and not merely by virtue of the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence.

Endowed with the similarity of the comprehension of the meaning of sentences such as "The Agnihotra [is to be performed]," the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence regarding the Agnihotra is of this nature because it is like the unborn ocean; thus,
the verbal realization of the True Brahman certainly becomes that which is to be enjoined.
If this is argued, [we reply]: no, for how could that [self-awareness] exist through dependence on the means of valid cognition and so forth?
It should be understood that [knowledge] is not something to be performed (vidheya), because it is subject to restraint by the will;
for even one who does not wish to go may still have the arising of the cognition of a foul odor.
It is not accepted by the authors of authentic scriptures that knowledge is something to be performed.
Indeed, the statements of the Vedānta bring about the knowledge of an indivisible reality; they produce a cognition that does not have a relational object—of this there is no doubt.
In that regard, all the words situated within the meaning of a single nominal stem— which convey the sense understood from that one nominal stem—
such as the words "Being" (satya), "Knowledge" (jñāna), and so forth, exist in the form of question and answer.
Just as the definition of "conjunction" (sahita) is stated as residing in the mere [object] itself—
such as from the sentence, "This moon is a preeminent, singular light"—
there is no doubt regarding the knowledge of the connection [of the object] through its uncommon property (asādhāraṇadharma) and so forth.
If it is argued that [the Self] is to be negated there because it consists of the seed of questions, we say no;
for this light here is preeminent, and if it were so, it would indeed be directly perceived.
"One who desires to know the division of the moon," "the moon," and "one possessed of the division of the moon"—
it is not logical for these to have that [same] meaning according to such a certainty. Indeed, the assumption is simply that they do not understand the meaning of the names.
If it is argued that the analogy here is to be understood as the union with the moon,
just as the union with Brahman is to be understood, then it is said in reply:
for the state of being Brahman consists precisely in being the locus of relation to all objects of perception.
Because it is stated, "That alone is one," thereby negating the knowledge of anything else;
because of the parsimony [of the doctrine] that all evils cease through the single cognition of That;
and because, in the view that asserts non-difference between the qualified Brahman (guṇabrahman) and the unqualified, there is the teaching of its union [with the Self].
Through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), it is difficult to find [a term] that does not involve the loss of its own primary meaning.
Because there is no difference between the properties, the substratum, and their relationship and so forth.
Therefore, there is no distinction whatsoever;
for that reason, it is also impossible [to establish a distinction] for one who delights in the doctrine of difference regarding a possessor of qualities such as omniscience.
Since the cognition of that [Brahman] arises through the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of effects such as the earth and so forth,
and since all that is worldly must be understood as Brahman distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*),
there are three limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

In the state of deep sleep (*supti*), ignorance (*avidyā*) is indeed the object of knowledge; the first [form] consists of the adjunct (*upādhi*) delimited by the connection with suffering and so forth, while the second consists of the form of the adjunct conjoined with that which is reflected in the primary [intellect]. The intellect of the one born after that [state] is the second.

Its nature as a third-order adjunct is well known; and for the sake of the realization of the inner self, superimposition (adhyāsa) is defined as the cognition of another's attributes in something else, which is an immeasurable delusion.

The definition of superimposition (adhyāsa) exists in four modes: as superimposition with its defining characteristics, as false superimposition, as mutual superimposition, and as real superimposition. Among these, by contact with fire...

Just as water possesses the power of burning through proximity to fire, so too the gross body— possessing the powers characterized by going, seeing, thinking, and knowing through proximity to the inner self—
is called a false superimposition (*mithyādhyāsa*). Through the superimposition of non-difference from the gross body, [one thinks] "I..."

The superimposition of bodily attributes such as "I go" and so forth [occurs] upon the inner self; the group of sense organs [is superimposed] upon the inner self. This is called mutual superimposition (*itarādhyāsa*).
The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—the fundamental ego-sense (*mūlāhaṃkāra*)—constitutes the superimposition of reality (*satyādhyāsa*). Immediately thereafter, the notion "I" arises.

The superimposition of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) upon one another without any limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika-adhyāsa*) is said to be like that of a rope and a snake.

By the expression "I am the agent" (*ahaṃ kartā*), the superimposition of the attributes of the ego-sense and the self upon one another with a limiting adjunct (*sopādhika-adhyāsa*) is said to be like that of a red crystal. By the expression "I desire" (*icchāmyaham*), [the superimposition] of the attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the self [is indicated].
The superimposition of those attributes is said to be like the reflection of a bird reflected in the water of a flowing stream;
by the expression "I am a householder," the superimposition of a mere relationship—such as that of self, son, and so forth—is said to be like the conventional usage of figures in a painting. Thus...

Through the very process of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon the changeless Self, the conceptualization of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) occurs. In that regard, by superimposing external attributes upon the Self— such as "I am whole" or "I am deficient" due to the completeness or deficiency of children, wife, and so forth— one thinks, "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am walking," or "I am leaping."
Having superimposed the body and its attributes, and having superimposed the attributes of the sense organs— such as "I am one-eyed," "I am mute," or "I am deaf"—

and having superimposed the attributes of the internal organ— such as "I am the doer" and "I am the enjoyer"— through a lack of discrimination between them, one attributes the attributes of each to the other.
The inner self (pratyagātman), having superimposed the identity of the ego with the intellect and the mutual non-difference between them,

and having become established in the natural worldly usage of "I," "this," and "mine," mounts the chariot of the body— which is driven by the horses of the senses that have been brought under control— and proceeds as a mental modification.
The great chariot, skillful in traversing various kinds of sensory objects and regions, having enjoyed the various fruits obtainable therein,
delights as the preeminent one in a substratum that is unfit to be its own support.
The general definition of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is "being perceived.
Alternatively, the definition of illusory superimposition (*prātibhāsika-adhyāsa*) is "being perceived while being produced by a defect other than ignorance (*avidyā*)."

The summary [of the definition] is as follows: either "being perceived while residing in consciousness conditioned by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of 'this' (*idam*), which has as its object a sphere not impaired by a modification whose object is unknown," or "being produced by a defect other than ignorance (*avidyā*). These are the five states.

Furthermore, there are five states: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, the fourth (turiya), and that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta). Among these, in the gross body—which consists of the twenty-four principles (tattvas) comprising the ten gross elements, the ten sense organs, the five vital breaths (prāṇas), and the fourfold internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—[the waking state occurs].

That the Universal Soul (Viśvātman), the individual soul (Jīva), and the Lord known as Virāṭ become one, and while abiding in the heart-lotus— the locus of the eyes, time, and the presiding deity Viṣṇu, which consists of the letters representing the forms and qualities of the *satva*—
experiences the enjoyment of objects such as women through the totality of all the sense organs; that [is what is meant].

The waking state (*jāgrad-avasthā*). Furthermore, among those twenty-four principles (*tattva*), having set aside the five gross elements and the two—mind (*citta*) and intellect (*buddhi*)—the syllable *ukāra*, which is the quality of passion (*rajo-guṇa*), resides in the subtle body consisting of the remaining seventeen principles; it is presided over by Brahmā.

When the luminous individual soul (taijasajīva), having moved through the throat-center of the deity and the pericarp of the heart-lotus, becomes unified with the Lord known as Sūtrātman, it remains experiencing the enjoyment of objects through the impressions of the waking state by means of the mental organ;
this is called the state of dream. Furthermore, all around...
Accepting morsels of food for his young ones, placing all his offspring within the shade of his own wings,
and— like a peacock that has fallen asleep in one place— confining all their activities within himself,
he remains without fixed station upon the support of his own self, which is imbued with those latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).

The individual soul (prājña-jīva), whose nature consists of the existing primordial matter (prakṛti), whose cause is the body, whose quality is tamas, whose syllable is 'a', and whose presiding deity is Rudra—
moving within the center of the pericarp of that lotus located in the heart—
and the Lord known as the Inner Ruler (antaryāmī), both becoming one, experience the enjoyment of the object that is the bliss of Brahman.

That which exists as experiencing through the subtle instrument (*sūkṣmakaraṇa*) consisting of the function of *māyā* is the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Immediately following this are the states of waking and so forth— the three states, the three abodes, the three locations, and the three cities.

The states of *ūpāvasthā* (subsidiary states) are indeed associated with the various stages (*paryāya-nāma*). Furthermore, in the waking state, having abandoned that lotus and rendered the mind free from activity, one remains contemplating the nature of Brahman; this is what [is meant].

The state of the Fourth (turya) is so called; one should know that states such as fainting (mūrchā) and the like are also the state of the Fourth. That state in which one exists with the mind absorbed in the Self is the state beyond the Fourth (turyātīta). Furthermore, among those states, the state of deep sleep (suṣupti) belongs to stationary beings (sthāvara), both dreaming and deep sleep belong to animals (paśu), and [the waking state] belongs to the deities (devatā).
There is constant wakefulness. For ordinary human beings, there are three states; for those afflicted by epilepsy, there is the fourth state (turya);
and for the supreme masters of yoga, there is the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). Among these, the first three states manifest spontaneously for humans and are of the nature of saṃsāra.
Having come into being, they persist; having produced two remaining states through the power of yoga practice, they exist as means for liberation.
This is the falsity of states.
Furthermore, among those states, because no other state exists within any single one, they are all illusory;
whereas that which is woven through all those states, in all places and at all times,
is the innermost, pure consciousness-nature— the true essence of one's own fourth state (turyātman).
Furthermore, the proof of the self:
it is well known that cognition exists during the waking and dreaming states.
That cognition also exists in deep sleep is established by the fact that, immediately after arising from deep sleep, one has the recollection: "I slept happily."

The recollection of the two types of blissful ignorance during sleep— namely, "I knew nothing"— is not possible without an experience occurring at the time of deep sleep; therefore, by the means of valid cognition known as *arthāpatti* (presumption),
it is established that during deep sleep, the Self perceives the darkness that veils all objects such as jars, just as the eye perceives [objects].
Ignorance (avidyā) is that which veils all effects such as the entire body; and from such ignorance, within the subtle functions [of the mind], there arise—

like a mere fragment of moonlight flickering among the leaves of a most tremulous tree— moments of the portion of one's own essential bliss, whose nature alternates between appearing and being suppressed, and which depend upon other instruments [of perception].

By the phrase "experiences without [objects]," it is established that in that state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), consciousness remains stable. Immediately thereafter, through the recollection "I slept happily without knowing anything," there occurs— in sequence— a cognition of the absence of objects,
the cessation of the suffering of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), and the total absence of ignorance (*avidyā*) in deep sleep.

If it is argued that there exists a self consisting of bliss as a witness, and if it is asked why no one there thinks "I know," the reason is this: just as it is impossible for someone diving into a pond to say whether they possess a certain object or not without first emerging from the water, so it is in the state of deep sleep.

Even though cognition exists, it is not possible for the Self— which is the witness of all states— to adorn itself with the objects known by it while in the waking state, without the attainment of the cooperation of the instruments (the senses), due to the influence of time and karma;
such being the case, [it remains as the witness].

The nature of the Self as being self-luminous existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*) is established by direct experience. What is the proof for the reality of the Self? [It is stated in] the Śruti: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Bliss, Infinite, Auspicious, and Immutable."

In accordance with the principle of strengthening (bṛṃhaṇā), its reality must be accepted, and the Self must be admitted by all proponents of liberation to be of an eternally real nature. Nor should it be argued that the Self is unreal because it is an object (padārtha), like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; for in this case, "being perceptible" (dṛśyatva) is the limiting condition (upādhi). The Self is indeed perceptible.
Because it possesses consciousness whose object is the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), that which is not so is not this [Brahman], just as the phenomenal world and the like are not;

by this, the view of the Naiyāyikas and others is also refuted. Brahman is consciousness whose object is everything, but it is not the substratum of the consciousness whose object is everything, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, consciousness is well-established in all beings.

Because he is the locus of supreme love, the Self is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*); and because of the scriptural corroboration stating that "this too is another form of bliss," the Self possesses happiness.

In the statement "bliss is the Self," by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), bliss itself is the Self. Thus, the Self—unattached, indifferent, and of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss—is self-luminous.
Luminosity (*prakāśatva*) consists in not being cognizable by a consciousness that is either delimited by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) or undelimited by it;

for, since consciousness is one, the dual status of being both the object of cognition and the cognizer is impossible. Through such inquiry, [one realizes] the nature of the supreme Śiva, who is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), the witness (*sākṣin*) of all attributes of the vital breath and mind as well as their superimpositions, and who is unchanging and indifferent (*asaṅgoddāsīna*).

It is established by means of scriptural passages that censure duality and others that the non-dual Brahman is the Self (*ātman*), and it is likewise established that the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
For this very reason, it is said in the Āgamas: "The body is declared to be the temple; the *jīva* is the deity, Sadāśiva.
One should discard the floral offering of ignorance and worship with the realization 'I am He'. [Furthermore,] there is sleep within the *liṅga*.
And likewise in the Vāmana Purāṇa, there is a verse [supporting] that [it is] to be known from the expansion of the Śruti.
Then that Hari, the immutable Self, [beheld] Him who lies within the lotus of his heart.
Murāri manifested the Īśvara-liṅga to the gods;
the Lord, the illuminator of all, resides within the minds of all living beings.

Thus, from the corroboration provided by the *Kaṭhavallī* and other texts, it is established that the self-luminous identity of the inner Self (*pratyag-ātman*) with Brahman— signified by such terms as "Lord" (*īśvara*) and "Beginningless" (*anādi*)— dwells within the heart of all beings, O Arjuna.
And because of the scriptural corroboration that "the person here is self-luminous."
The Discrimination of the Five Sheaths:

Immediately following this are the five sheaths known as the annamaya (consisting of food), prāṇamaya (consisting of vital breath), manomaya (consisting of mind), vijñānamaya (consisting of consciousness), and ānandamaya (consisting of bliss).
Among these, the gross body produced from the semen and blood of the mother and father is indeed the annamaya-kośa.

Thus it is said: the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the winds, and the organs of action, when combined within the subtle body (*sūkṣma-tanu*), are called the sheath consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya-kośa*). The mind (*manas*) and the organs of cognition, when combined, are called the sheath consisting of mind (*manomaya-kośa*).
The ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which resembles an iron spearhead, is joined with the reflection of the consciousness of the inner self (*pratyagātma-caitanya*).
