Accompanied by the organs of knowledge, it is called the *vijñānamaya-kośa* (the sheath consisting of consciousness).
In the waking state of ignorance, which takes the form of the causal body (*kāraṇa-deha*),
there arise, in succession, pleasure, delusion, and joy through the sight, proximity, and union with undesirable objects such as women.
Thus, these three combined constitute this much—the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*).
[The following] verse refutes the notion that the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is the Self:
[The nature of the sheath consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya-kośa*) is that the ego alone is the Self.]
By those devoid of the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, it is expressed through the perception of one's own experience as "I am that" (*so'ham*).

The ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which consists of the sheath of consciousness (*vijñānamaya-kośa*), is indeed designated by the word "Self"; for those lacking the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self, it is the object of the cognition "I am that."

It is said: that [expression] "it is pleasing" is not like "blue lotus" and so forth; for in "blue lotus," "blue" is to be known as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and "lotus" as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). However, in the cognition "I am thin," the body is the qualifier of that consciousness through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), while the self exists in the state of being the qualificand.

Even in the cognition "I am the hearer" and "I am the meditator," the sense-organ (*indriya*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkṛti*) are presented there as qualifiers (*prakāra*), while the self (*ātman*) is to be understood as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), according to how it appears in that cognition. Now, [one might object]:

here, [the definition of verbal cognition] would be "a verbal cognition whose qualifier is the meaning of a nominal stem related by the relation of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka-sambandha*) through the relation of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā-sambandha*)."

According to the view of the Grammarians (Vaiyyākaraṇas), the cause [of verbal cognition] is the mental presentation (upasthiti) produced by a word co-occurring with that name, occurring at the time when a subsequent meaningful case-ending is presented to the already cognized and delimited [object].

Alternatively, according to the view of the modern Naiyāyikas, in cases such as "a blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*), the cause of a verbal cognition whose qualificandum is the meaning of a noun and whose relation is the delimiting relation (*avacchedaka-saṃsarga*) is the mental presentation (*upasthiti*) produced by a word that is co-occurrent with that noun, which is meaningful and expects that noun, and is distinct from the case-ending (*vibhakti*) associated with it.

If it is asked how there can be a relational cognition (*anvayabodha*) in cases such as "I am thin" (*kṛśo'ham*), given that the body qualified by thinness and the self—which is of the nature of consciousness—are distinct, we reply: such a relational cognition is possible at a time when there is no manifestation of difference; however, this is not the case in the instance of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

There is no contradiction, because the sublation arising from a defect occurs only due to the production of such a cognition; the example of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*) and the like is based merely on the possession of the same grammatical case-ending. Even though there are four types of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), a relational cognition (*anvayabodha*) is possible through the juxtaposition of words with identical case-endings. For instance, in the case of repetition: *...* [text fragment] *...abhyāse* (in the case of repetition).
Alternatively, based on the fundamental scriptures, there is either identity through sublation (*bādhā*) or the status of being a qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*).
In cases such as "I am thin," there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) due to the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the name upon the gross body, the senses, the ego, and so forth.
In the case of "He who is the thief is the post," it is [coreferentiality] through sublation.

Grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs in identity, as in "That which is the individual soul (*jīva*), that is Brahman"; it occurs in the relation of qualifier and qualified through non-difference, as in "That which is blue, that is a lotus. This example is given in a general sense for such cases as "Name is Brahman," wherein name is [merely] nominally Brahman, but not so in reality.
Even though there is difference, for the sake of meditation, there is a concealment of the superimposed non-difference; likewise,
due to the power of beginningless ignorance and other veils,
the ego— which consists of the superimposition of non-difference upon gross difference and so forth— is not the Self, because it is an object of perception, like a pot.
The ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is not the self, because it is perceived as a qualification of the self,
just like the body, which is emaciated or stout.

Next follows the discrimination between the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and consciousness (caitanya). Thus, when it is asked how the insentient ego-sense can possess the capacity to cognize external objects, [the answer is given]: like the movement of a needle due to its proximity to a magnet, or as in the case of heat.

Just as a mirror held in hand reveals the light and darkness located in its corners through the proximity of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), so too the reflection of consciousness exists within itself; by this means,
the insentient ego (*ahaṃkāra*) alone is made to move through the states of waking and dreaming as the knower of external objects.

The meaning is that in deep sleep (suṣupti) one becomes dissolved and devoid of activity. When it is asked what the metaphor for that expansion [of the world] is, [it is said]: within the corner consisting of ignorance—which has the state of the dissolution of the ego (ahaṃkāra) as its limit—one's own self exists like a motionless lamp, situated against the wall within the door-panel consisting of sleep.
That which exists while manifesting by itself is this light of the inner self (*pratyagātma-jyotis*). [Commentary:

Immediately thereafter, through the accumulation of the attainment of the impelling force of the collection of winds such as time and karma, there occurs the crossing over the barrier of sleep, which was acting like a door-panel of incomparable, present darkness.
Upon the threshold of the *mahat-tattva*— which consists of the first stage of primordial ignorance (*avidyā*) that is the root of diverse effects and causes and arises immediately after the Truth—
is placed a crystal gem composed of the *sāttvika-ahaṃkāra*, [distinguished] from the inert, unreal *ahaṃkāra* and other such factors.
Containing within it the reflection of the lamp of the inner self (pratyagātman) which shines forth in opposition [to all objects],
having become Śiva as before, and illuminating the middle chamber consisting of the dream state, he [proceeds] upward.
Having emerged outside through the windows of the sense-faculties— the overseers who bring security through the power of wisdom—
it remained illuminating the courtyard area outside the peaked hall that constitutes the waking state;
yet, by the very impulsion of the winds of time, karma, and other factors, it became firmly fixed once again within the door-panel characterized by sleep.

When that [ego] was bound, and at that very moment the crystal-gem of the ego dissolved into its own cause, which is ignorance (avidyā), the two houses situated in the middle of the courtyard outside the waking and dreaming states became filled with darkness.
Then, the light of the lamp of consciousness reflected in that crystal-gem of the ego— its own...

It exists unified within the lamp of the inner self, which is its fundamental ground. Thus, having understood the presence and absence of the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) amidst the three states beginning with waking, the immutable Self is established as one that exists individually apart from the body and so forth; by this, it is proven that the ego (ahaṃkāra) is not the Self.
The verse concerning the connection with the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
The Self is the inward consciousness of the conscious Self with respect to those things that have become external objects.
And [it is established] by such forms as "the object of knowledge" (vedya) and so forth, consisting of both the insentient and the sentient.
This side of the mirror [is that] which faces away from the face.

Similarly, the luminous ego (ahaṃkāra) has a connection with three factors: the body, the reflection of consciousness (cit-chāyā), and the inner self (pratyagātman). Among these, by the expression "I am feverish," there is a connection with the ego as it is joined with the reflection of consciousness.

The very capacity of the gross body to perceive heat and so forth, being produced by karma, is called "born of karma" (*karmaja*). Immediately thereafter, the connection between the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyā*) and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*)— expressed as "I know"— is said to be "innate" (*sahaja*), because it remains without destruction from the beginning of creation until liberation.

Immediately following this, by the phrase "I am the agent," the connection between the unattached inner self (*pratyagātman*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is said to be born of delusion; thus, all such [distinctions] take the form of a discrimination from the visible world.
This is the relationship of the original object and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*).
Immediately thereafter, Paraśiva, whose nature is the Brahman that is attributeless and pure consciousness, is the original object (*bimba*);
primordial *māyā* is the mirror; and the *liṅga* of Īśvara, whose nature is Brahman with attributes, is the reflection (*pratibimba*).
Furthermore, that same Paraśiva is the original object, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the mirror, and the *jīva-liṅga* is the reflection.
Furthermore, the Liṅga of Īśvara alone is the original object (bimba); Māyā, whose nature is the equilibrium of the Guṇas, is the mirror;
and the manifestation of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa-prapañca) is the reflection. Subsequently, the Liṅga of the individual soul (jīva) alone is the original object;
the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the mirror; and objects such as pleasure and so forth are the reflections. Thus it is.

When both the individual witness (jīvasākṣin) and the Lord-witness (īśvarasākṣin)— which are respectively the unconditioned original and its reflection— exist, the logical possibility of their identity arises.
Regarding the reflection of a formless object:

if it is asked how a formless entity can be reflected so clearly immediately thereafter, it is explained by the analogy that even though space is formless, it is reflected in water; thus, the principle of reflection applies here as well.
When that power of consciousness exists, it becomes contradictory.

Even if it is logically accepted that the reflection of a reflection is itself a reflection of the original object (*bimba*), how can God, being the very form of the universe, be said to be reflected? To this it is replied: by being reflected in a mirror.
Like the reflection of the sun's orb in a wall, it is merely an appearance of duality; thus, the contradiction does not appear in any way whatsoever.
The destruction of the similarity with the reflection (bimba):
immediately thereafter, when it is asked how stainless consciousness became a stained appearance of consciousness,
[the answer is that] the face, though beautiful in its stainlessness, appears marked in a mirror due to the extremely thin layer of mercury [on its surface].
When it is stated that just as a reflection becomes stained,

so too the very fact that the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as māyā and avidyā possess the quality of being stains constitutes the cause for the appearance of consciousness (cidābhāsa), the doctrine that everything existing as a reflection is identical to the original object (bimba) is thereby refuted.
If it is argued that there is thus an identity of conditions (*upādhi-sāmya*), then in response to the question "Of what is the reflection invariably concomitant?", it is stated:
in the absence of the mirror serving as the condition, there is an absence of that [reflection]; when the mirror exists, there is its existence; provided that [the mirror] is not impaired.

The defect of a reflection in a mirror is as follows: when the mirror moves, the reflection moves; when the mirror is broken, the reflection itself becomes broken and merges with the mirror which serves as its source. Thus, the reflection is strictly co-extensive with its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Therefore, [this applies] to the limiting adjunct of ignorance in the form of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

When the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is joined with impurities such as desire and anger, the nature of the individual soul (jīvaliṅga-svarūpa) becomes stained; however, when the internal organ is purified through dispassion and discrimination characterized by the cultivation of friendliness and other virtues,
the nature of the individual soul becomes stainless like the emblem of Śiva (śivaliṅga), once the internal organ has been dissolved.
It is certain that upon death, due to the destruction of the individual life-force (*jīvatva*), one becomes one with the *śivaliṅga*.

Furthermore, while the substrate (*upadheya*) is distinct, consciousness (*caitanya*) is indeed one; it is merely through its proximity that the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as *māyā* and the rest, become active.

When it is thus stated that consciousness (caitanya) exists pervading all directions and time, and it is asked how its effects— conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi)— do not manifest as universal and eternal, [the answer is given] by way of the analogy of the various limited sounds of the vīṇā, flute, mṛdaṅga drum, and so forth, within a single undivided space (ākāśa).

Since there exists a variety of words distinguished by mutual difference— just as a distinction is conceived for the modified space (ākāśa) such that one speaks of "the space within a lute," "the space within a flute," or "the space within a drum"— so too,
through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the respective internal organs, bodies, and so forth, there is a differentiation of the consciousness of each individual soul (jīva).
It is stated that the distinction between bondage and liberation is established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

Following the "six beginningless factors" (*anādi-ṣaṭka*), there is the Supreme Śiva, whose nature is pure consciousness; he is the Supreme Lord who is the cause of the universe and yet appears as a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*).

The individual soul (jīva), ignorance which is the root of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord (jīveśvara-bheda), and the distinction between consciousness and the insentient (cijjaḍa-bheda)— these six are established as beginningless. When it is asked how the Supreme Lord produced the phenomenal world (prapañca) along with these [six] in the absence of a cause, it is not merely that there is no production of the aforementioned six beginningless entities.

However, since the creation of the world— consisting of space and so forth, which is non-substantial yet not as unreal as a rabbit's horn, and which is indeterminable like the silver imagined in a mother-of-pearl shell by a living being— proceeded from the Supreme Lord, its being fashioned by the Supreme Lord remains unrefuted.
The seven stages are:
immediately thereafter,
[the states of] ignorance-obscuration, distraction, indirect knowledge, direct knowledge, cessation of sorrow, and unimpeded satisfaction.

By that very [ignorance], there are seven states of the individual soul (*jīva*); among them, the *jīva*, which is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) attached to *saṃsāra*, does not know its own innate nature—the self-luminous inner self (*pratyagātman*)—prior to the inquiry into the meaning of the scriptures. Immediately thereafter, at one point in time...

When there is an attachment to the conscious self (cidātman), the two-fold delusion that "the inner self does not exist" and "the inner self does not shine forth" is called the veil (āvaraṇa), which is the effect of that ignorance (ajñāna). Thinking "I am myself the doer of action" and "I am myself the enjoyer of the fruit of action," the individual soul (jīva) as a reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), identifying with the body, is itself the distraction (vikṣepa).

Thus it is said: immediately thereafter, through faith in the scriptures and the words of the teacher which establish the existence of the Self, the very realization that "the inner Self exists" is called the immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) that removes the description of non-existence; [this occurs] when [one realizes] "you yourself are Brahman."

The very thorough knowledge that "I am indeed the inner self," arising through the ripening of the inquiry into the Vedic sentences that serve as the means of instruction, is called immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), which brings about the cessation of the description of the second [illusory] identification.
Immediately thereafter, following the direct realization of the inner self, [the notions] "I am the agent of action" and "I am the enjoyer of the fruit" [cease].

The cessation of grief is said to be precisely the relinquishing of the nature of suffering characterized by the fear of living. Thereafter, all that was to be done has been accomplished and the entire collection of fruits to be attained has been obtained; thus, one attains natural contentment.

Attaining the state of abiding [in the Self] alone is called unbridled satisfaction (*niraṅkuśatṛpti*). These two states—the cessation of sorrow and unbridled satisfaction—are the very fruits of direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*). This is the synthesis of the seven stages.

Immediately following this, when it is asked what example there is for the fact that the manifestation of the seven states, such as ignorance (*ajñāna*), is impossible within that Supreme Self— since the Self, whose nature is consciousness, is self-luminous and eternally immediate— the [text] states: "Previously, ten men, having crossed a single river..."

Immediately after departing, at the time of attaining his own reflection, the man who remains counting those nine men while failing to recognize himself as the tenth man— that very state is called ignorance; [it is said that] "the tenth does not exist" and "he does not appear."

Thus, obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) is indeed the effect of ignorance. Immediately thereafter, the sorrow that "the tenth person has died in the river" is called distraction (*vikṣepa*). Immediately after that, through the separate word of one reliable person, the thorough knowledge that "the tenth person exists" [arises], whereas [previously] there was the notion that "the tenth does not exist."

The knowledge that contradicts the first enclosure is called indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*). Immediately thereafter, the very abandonment of the suffering of death in the tenth [enclosure] is called the cessation of sorrow (*śokanivṛtti*). Immediately thereafter, by virtue of one's own abiding state, there is indeed the true being (*sadbhāva*) through bliss.
There arises satisfaction free from restraint.
Regarding the inquiry into the sentences of the Vedas:
when it is asked how this inquiry into the sentences of the Vedas proceeds, there are injunctive sentences and prohibitive sentences.

A Vedic sentence that conveys a goal to be accomplished exists in three forms. Among these, a sentence in which words such as "one should perform" (*yajeta*) are co-occurrent with "sacrifice" and so forth is an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*). In that regard, according to the view of Bhaṭṭapāda, the meaning of the word "one should" (*ājñā*) co-occurrent with the root *yaji* (to sacrifice) is an *bhāvanā* (productive activity) whose instrument (*karaṇa*) is a sacrifice named by some specific term.

According to the view of the Guru (Prabhākara), the meaning of an injunctive sentence (*vidhivākya*) is that "the task (*kārya*) has sacrifice as its object," which is the *apūrva* qualified by the state of being a task (*kāryatva*). According to the view of the Naiyāyikas,

the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) as co-occurring with the injunctive suffix is that "sacrifice is a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhana*), namely, the state of being a means to a desired end and the state of being achievable through volitional effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) residing in the sacrifice.

According to the Vaiyākaraṇa school, the threefold meaning— consisting of being a means to the desired, not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence, and being enjoined by the Veda— is the sense of the verbal root when it is used in conjunction with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).

This refers to the performance of the action denoted by the verbal root, such as sacrificing, which is characterized as a means to the desired and is performed by an agent who possesses the requisite qualification for that ritual act.

The meaning of a verbal root such as *yaj* (to sacrifice) when uttered in conjunction with an optative suffix (*āva*) is [an injunction]. A sentence possessing such a meaning is an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*). A prohibitive sentence (*niṣedha-vākya*) is defined as an injunctive sentence uttered in conjunction with the negative particle *nañ*, such as "one should not drink liquor," "one should not eat *kalañja*," or "one should not kill a Brahmin."

A collection of statements that is devoid of injunctions such as those concerning birth (*ajādi-vidhi*), which forms a single syntactical unity with positive injunctions, and which establishes the identity of the real Brahman and the Self, is called a statement that conveys an established fact (*siddhārtha-bodhaka-vākya*).
This is the meaning of the great Vedānta statements.

Immediately thereafter, among the four Vedas consisting of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva, there are four great statements (*mahāvākya*) that sequentially establish the realization of the accomplished meaning: "Consciousness is Brahman" (*prajñānaṃ brahma*), "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), and "This self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*). Among these, the primary one is "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).

The sentence consists of three words: *tat*, *tvam*, and *asi*. The word *tat* is a nominal stem, the word *tvam* is a nominal stem, and the word *asi* is a verbal form; thus, these constitute the three words. In this authoritative statement, their three respective meanings are indeed "Śiva," "the individual soul (jīva)," and "the unity of those two"—this is the meaning of *tattvam*.
Since identity is already established merely by the co-utterance of the two words [tat and tvam], the word "asi" (are) is redundant;
for the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words "that" and "you" is obtained through their sharing the same case-ending.
And coreferentiality consists in two words having different grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) referring to a single object.

The conclusion stated by the author of the *Śiromaṇi* is as follows: the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of words consists in their capacity to present a single substratum (*ekadharmī*) through two distinct attributes (*dharmas*). If it is argued that, since identity is already obtained even without the word "asi" (sword), the word "asi" is redundant—[we reply]: no, for the word "asi" [is necessary].

The co-utterance [of the word] merely restates the unity already obtained through co-utterance, whereas the preceding statement is the co-utterance itself. All those situated in the *Pāñcarātra* [scriptures] provide the determination of the meaning of that word.
They act for the sake of that state; they are His servants and dependent upon Him.

And since there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "you are that servant," the occurrence of the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is equal for you as well. If it is argued that there is metaphorical indication in both words [for you], whereas for us there is only one in a single word;

If one were to admit a difference between the referents of the words *tat* (That) and *tvam* (Thou), there would follow the fault of infinite complexity (*ānantya-gaurava*) and the impossibility of attaining the reality taught by the scriptures of Truth (*tattva-śāstra*). To the question "How so? it has already been explained that when all worldly transactions are possible through a single Self alone, despite its various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), [there is no need for such a distinction].
Because it would entail the fault of the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating an infinite number of selves;
immediately thereafter, there is the triad of relations regarding the sentence-meaning: namely, those between words and word-meanings, and between words and sentence-meanings.

The three types of relationship— namely, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), and the relation between the indicated and the indicator (*lakṣyalakṣaṇabhāva*)— constitute the triad of relationships in their respective order;
these are the denotative meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam*.
Immediately thereafter, regarding the two meanings of the referents of the words *tat* and *tvam*— namely, the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*) and the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*)—

one should unify the Virāṭ-puruṣa, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Īśvara, who are the collective forms of the previously mentioned three subtle bodies (gross, etc.), with Brahman; and by contemplating them as one, like a red-hot iron ball, this pertains to the word *tat*.

The "denoted meaning" (vācyārtha) is called the primary meaning (mukhyārtha) or the literal meaning (abhidhārtha). Subsequently, when one contemplates the individual forms of the three bodies— Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña— together with the inner self (pratyagātman) as a single unity, like a heated iron ball, that is the denoted meaning and the primary meaning of the term *tvam* (the "thou").
It is called the "expressed meaning" (abhidhārtha).

The meaning indicated by the words *tat* and *tvam* is the reality; immediately thereafter, by distinguishing the Virāṭ-puruṣa and others, [it is shown that] Brahman alone, devoid of limiting adjuncts (nirupādhika), is the referent of the word *tat*.

The indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) is said to be the purified meaning of the word *tat*; subsequently, by discerning the universe and so forth, the very unconditioned inner self (*pratyagātman*) is said to be the indicated meaning of the word *tvam*, the purified meaning of the word *tvam*.

Indication (lakṣaṇā) is, in that context, a relation with the denotable meaning (śakyasaṃbandha). For example, in the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the word "Gaṅgā" has its primary power (śakti) in the river-current; by that power, it is the river-current that is conveyed by the word "Gaṅgā."
The flow is the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) of the word "Ganges," and its relation to the bank and so forth exists; that very [relation] is *lakṣaṇā*.

Now, one might object: the bank and such things related to the Ganges ought to be the primary meaning of the word "Ganges," because they are what is recalled by the word "Ganges" through its co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with [the word "bank"].

If it is argued that the word *gaṅgā* has a direct denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the bank, because it is the counter-correlate of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) [of the bank], just like a flowing stream; or alternatively, that the word *gaṅgā* is directly denotative of the bank, because it causes the recollection of the bank as the counter-correlate of the syntactic connection [with the word] *ghoṣa*, just like the word *tīra*—we say no. For if the word *gaṅgā* were directly denotative of the bank, just like the word *tīra*, then [the cognition of the bank] would arise without the reflection upon the impossibility of the syntactic connection [of the word *gaṅgā*] with the bank.

It would be appropriate to apply [the term] to the bank, water, and so forth, and there would be an identical application; furthermore, there would be no need for the recognition of an unestablished intention (*tātparyānupapatti*). Therefore, the word "Ganges" does not possess a primary denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to the bank; rather, even without the operation of primary denotation, it [conveys the meaning] solely through its connection with the power residing in the flowing stream (*pravāha*), which is the basis of indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Because [the meaning] arises in dependence upon the bank, and because a word-meaning must be something not obtainable by other means— since it is not possible to assume multiple meanings for a single referent—
there is no difference in the mode of indication (lakṣaṇā).

Immediately thereafter, that indication (lakṣaṇā) itself becomes threefold— indication by exclusion (jahallakṣaṇā), indication by non-exclusion (ajahallakṣaṇā), and indication by both exclusion and non-exclusion (jahadajahallakṣaṇā)— with the three examples in sequence being: "A hamlet dwells in the Gaṅgā," "Spears enter," and "This is that Devadatta."

In those cases, there is *jahallakṣaṇā* (indication with abandonment), wherein the word "Gaṅgā" itself, because its own primary meaning in the form of a flowing stream is untenable as the locus for a hamlet and cowherds, abandons that [primary] sense and functions by indicating the bank.
The *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-abandoning indication) occurs immediately thereafter; the word "spear" (*kuṇta*), without abandoning its own primary meaning, indicates the men who carry spears.
By means of the *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (the indicative function that both excludes and includes),
the word "he" (*sa*) conveys Devadatta as qualified by past time, place, and age, while the word "this" (*ayam*) conveys him as qualified by present time, place, and age.

However, since the identity of two objects characterized by mutually contradictory properties is not possible, one must set aside the aspect of contradictory properties due to the temporal difference inherent in both objects, and—retaining only the non-contradictory aspect of Devadatta himself—one concludes: "This is that very person; that is this very person."

Thus, identity is established; this very [identity] is what is called *jahadajahallakṣaṇā* (the indicator that abandons and does not abandon [the primary meaning]), which is synonymous with *bhāgatyāgalakṣaṇā* (the indicator characterized by the abandonment of a part).
Furthermore, Arjuna and others are past entities, being the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of a present destruction (*dhvaṃsa*);
Kalki and others are future objects, being the counter-correlates of a present prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
A "present" entity is defined as any one of two entities existing at a time that is the locus of a mental construction (*bhāvanā*) not simultaneous with itself;
such an entity is said to be "either one" when it lacks the absence of both differences whose counter-correlates are delimited by properties that serve as the delimiters of contradictory entities.
Regarding the meaning of "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*),
when it is asked why this very sentence "This is that" (*so 'yam*) is suitable to be cited as an illustration for the statement "That thou art," [the answer is:
the word "That" (*tat*) refers to [Brahman] characterized by excellent qualities such as omniscience, which constitute its primary denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*).

It establishes Śiva as being beyond direct perception. Now, one might object: since the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states, "O Brahmin, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are the primary powers of Brahman," and because of scriptural passages establishing that the three forms are the powers of Brahman, Śiva is subordinate to Brahman and thus cannot be the referent of the term "That" (*tat*).

If it is asked how so, [the answer is that] by the word "Śiva," Paramaśiva is understood. Through the statement in the Śiva Purāṇa, which supplements the Atharvaśikhā, the status of Paramaśiva as the Supreme Brahman (parabrahma) is apprehended. For instance, there is this verse:
Because all this, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra, [is that].
Together with all the elements and the sense organs, it is first brought forth.
But he who is the meditator upon causes, the creator, is the supreme cause.
It is never produced from anything else, nor at any time.
Endowed with all sovereign powers and other perfections, he himself was known by the name Sarveśvara.
Śambhu, who dwells in the midst of space, is to be meditated upon by all those seeking liberation.

Thus, the status of Paraśiva as the referent of that word [tat] is established in both ways; meanwhile, the word "thou" (tvam) denotes the individual soul (jīva), who is characterized by qualities such as limited knowledge and is an immediate manifestation of consciousness. This [word "thou"]...
Since the identity of two entities possessing mutually contradictory attributes is impossible,

one must immediately thereafter discard the contradictory aspects of the attributes— such as perceptibility and so forth— belonging to both entities, and recognize the two referents indicated by the words (*lakṣyārtha*) as being non-contradictory, consisting solely of the nature of consciousness (*caitanyamātra*), and as the immutable Brahman.

Having accepted that "this is that" and "that is this," the word *asi* (art) becomes meaningful by establishing identity (*tādātmya*) between the two referents indicated by those terms, while simultaneously teaching that attributes such as mediacy (*parokṣatva*) and immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) are merely imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*). When this has occurred, [the nature] of the Self...

The nature of the meaning of the sentence is that there is established only the unbroken, single-flavored awareness (*akhaṇḍaikarasabodhamātra*). Following this, in the great sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), there is the oneness of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).

When asked "How so?", [the answer is: by setting aside the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the jar, just as [one says] "space is one alone"; by discarding the state of being a human in the case of Rāmacandra, just as [one says] "you yourself are Viṣṇu";
by negating the condition of being a hunter in the case of Karṇa, just as [one says] "you yourself are the son of Kuntī"; and by removing the suffering of death from the tenth person.
Just as in the statement "you yourself are the tenth," the natural establishment [of the fact] precludes the comprehension of the sentence-meaning through any intermediate process;
likewise, immediately thereafter, like the sentence "heaven belongs to one who offers a single flower," the *arthavāda* serves to produce an expectation regarding liberation (*mokṣa*).

[The opponent might argue that the statement] "the image is the form of the deity" is like a [descriptive] sentence; "the meditative passage" is like a sentence [of praise], such as "this man is Indra"; "it is figurative" is like a sentence addressed to an attendant, such as "the king [is here]"; "it is a similarity of qualities" is like a sentence such as "this boy is fire"; and "this is the body of the cow."

It refers to genus and individual, like the sentence "clay is nothing other than the jar"; it refers to cause and effect, like the sentence "a blue lotus"; it refers to quality and the possessor of quality, like the sentence "there is a difference between milk and curd";
it refers to modification, like the sentence "the water-drops are one"; and it refers to part and whole.

Just as there is identity between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), so too is there the relation of original and reflection; having thus conceptualized it in many ways with a focus on difference, one must speak [of the truth]:
"Non-duality is real; non-duality is from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*); he who perceives multiplicity goes to death. He who...
He who perceives diversity does not know that; it is one, there is neither duality nor multiplicity, there is no division whatsoever here.
Indeed, there is only one; Rudra is one; it is truly one without a second. He perceives this oneness.
The true meaning [of the scriptures] is that there is a contradiction with such Vedic passages as "Auspicious non-duality is the fourth," and "That is full, this is full," and so forth;
immediately after [this realization], [the distinction between the two ceases].

Through the authority of scripture, the teacher, one’s own experience, and reasoning, the true meaning is determined: that the Śiva-liṅga, which is the referent of the word *tat*, is indeed the jīva-liṅga, which is the referent of the word *tvam*.
This is not inconsistent with [the doctrine of] illusoriness (*mithyātva*).
Immediately after stating that non-duality (advaita), which constitutes the qualifying portion [of the definition], is false,
and having stated that non-duality is established when the identity of the real, pure consciousness alone is asserted—
if it is asked how non-duality is not tenable because falsity has no other recourse— [the answer is: because the world is false.

Granted that falsity (mithyātva) resides in the world, since there can be no existence without a substratum; yet, if it is said that it resides in Śiva, that is not tenable because Śiva is of the nature of truth (satya). Now, if it is argued that falsity itself is the truth, then since Śiva is the one [truth] and that falsity is the one truth, two truths would arise; therefore, it must be "only one."

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the scriptures (*śruti*). Moreover, if it is said that "the false is false," then by stating the truth of one between the true and the false, the other must be negated; for when one thing is false, the other will necessarily be true. Thus, having seen silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, [one might wonder] whether this is silver or not.

If it is argued that when one who was previously doubting—thinking "is it this or that?"—subsequently determines [the object], there is an experience of the existence of falsity within the phenomenal world (prapañca), and that if the prapañca were real, then the reality of non-duality (advaita) would be lost; we say no. For example, when a person standing at a distance sees an elephant and doubts whether it is a horse or a buffalo, a farmer standing nearby [knows] "this is not [a horse or a buffalo]."

Once it is certain that [the elephant] is a buffalo, just as the state of being a horse in that same elephant will subsequently not be true, so too the falsity of a falsehood is not contradictory; yet, that falsehood, having never ceased to be false, never exists in the form of truth. If one asks why, it is because it is an unreal object (*alīka-vastu*).

Even that which appears as if it were certain is ultimately false; indeed, it remains nothing but false, for the nature of the false never appears as certainty. Therefore, when the duality appearing through various modifications is destroyed, that knowledge itself—just as fire, having consumed the forest, is itself [extinguished]—[ceases].

As if destroyed and having gone to destruction, it is as though born anew; moreover, since that which has become its support— the first substratum— is known as the one true Śiva-consciousness, there is certainly no loss whatsoever in stating this.

When it is asked: "If false knowledge exists, how can there be the establishment of truth? Furthermore, in the Vedāntic position which demonstrates the falsity of the entire phenomenal world, how is the attainment of liberation—which consists of this very truth—possible through the inquiry into the Śruti?"
The experience of sexual union with a woman in a delusory dream, the falling of one’s virility due to reality,
the attainment of genuine accomplishments such as prosperity through the worship of imagined deities like the stone Bhairava,
and reflections in a mirror that do not correspond to the original object— all these [are examples].

Just as the vision of true beauty occurs through hearing the words of one who is untrue, so too is the attainment of ultimate liberation [achieved] by means of the scriptural word, even though it is unreal.

Now, [it may be argued that] on account of the identity between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), such unreality is untenable; nor can their identity be established through the experience of their difference—as in the case of Caitra and his reflection—given the perception of duality in water and other media. How then [can there be identity]?
It must be stated that the reflection of Caitra’s face ought to be distinct from Caitra’s face itself,
because it possesses properties such as facing toward [the observer] which are contradictory to the properties residing in Caitra’s face,
just like the reflection of another face; this is established by the experience, "I see my face in the mirror."

In the case of the cognition "this [reflection] is indeed situated in the neck," since there is no experience of the absence of the face in the mirror— characterized by its non-existence there— and of the relation of "facedness" to it, multiple cognitions would be invalid even in your own position, due to the non-difference between the state of being situated in the neck and its substratum.
There would follow the consequence of invalidity for various cognitions such as those of teeth and hair of this kind;

furthermore, there is the conceptual complexity of postulating a substratum (*dharmikalpanāgaurava*), and because there is an absence of causes for the production and cognition of reflections of stars, clouds, and so forth, which are perceived as being located in many distant places.
Therefore, since a reflection is observed even of the sun and other objects that lack a shadow— distinct from the well-known shadow characterized by clear teeth and so forth—
the term "shadow" (chāyā) is used figuratively because its movement is dependent on the movement of the original object (bimba), and not through any logical necessity.

One also experiences "the face in the mirror" by superimposing upon the very face of the original image its distinctness from what resides in the mirror and its orientation toward oneself. Nor should it be argued that, in accordance with this cognition, there exists another face in the mirror—
like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell— for such a cognition can be explained otherwise.

If it is argued that one perceives, "I see this face located in the mirror as being on my neck; this is not a separate face," thereby negating the connection [of the face] with the mirror while experiencing its non-difference from the well-known face— otherwise, one would experience "this is not my face" just as one experiences "this is not silver"— then [the case of the reflection] is similar, even though the identity of the original object (*bimba*) and the reflection (*pratibimba*) is real.
Since qualities such as being oriented toward oneself are illusory, their reality has been stated;
just as the beauty and other attributes of a face are perceived when it is real, so too,
through the investigation of the scriptures concerning the illusory nature [of the self], the attainment of liberation in the ultimate sense occurs.
Regarding the establishment of stainlessness (*nirañjanatva*):

immediately following this, when it is stated—given that Śiva, who is denoted by the *praṇava*, is the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe—how does the destruction of suffering born from ignorance regarding pure consciousness (*śuddhacinmātra*) occur through knowledge of Him? Thus it was asked.
Just as the illusory silver appearing due to the absence of knowledge regarding mother-of-pearl does not perish through the cognition of crystal without the subsequent cognition of mother-of-pearl,
so too the world is not destroyed without the knowledge of Paraśiva; and that Paraśiva [remains].

If it were an object of knowledge (*jñānaviṣaya*), there would be a loss of its being beyond the reach of speech and mind (*avāṅmanasagocaratva*), and it would result in its having specific attributes (*saviśeṣatva*).
If you accept this as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), then scriptural passages such as "Śiva is partless, stainless, auspicious, and peaceful" would be contradicted.
Therefore, when it is said that the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is thus inconsistent (*asamañjasa*), the sweet flavor [of truth] remains perfectly intact.

When this is said, just as rightness (samyaktva) is not distinct from that [reality], so too the supreme Brahman, the consciousness of Śiva, whose sole nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, is untainted— like a lotus leaf free from the adhesion of water— and, because duality has been cast far away, it is stainless; in that Śiva, stainlessness is first established as being free from all defects.

Just as a rope is known upon the object being perceived through the words of a trustworthy person as if it were directly present, so too the Supreme Lord— who is the cause of the worlds and is accompanied by *māyā*—
is known as Śiva, the supreme Brahman, who is free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), stainless (*nirañjana*), non-dual (*advitīya*), and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). He is the *liṅga*.

The conclusion— that the cessation of suffering occurs through the immediate (aparokṣa) verbal knowledge produced by the sentences of Vedānta, because there is a commonality of object between knowledge and ignorance— is thus faultless.

Furthermore, regarding the proof of the attributeless (nirguṇa) nature: since Brahman is endowed with attributes through inference and other means supported by worldly logic, the establishment of its attributelessness is not possible; thus it has been stated that "Brahman has the scripture as its source, it is the witness, the knower, and absolute."

By the scriptural authority of such passages as "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇa), [Brahman] becomes known solely through the means of verbal testimony (śabda); by this, the means of inference (anumāna) imagined by disputants is refuted.
Therefore, following the doctrine taught by Paraśiva among those who established the tradition of Brahmavidyā, beginning with Brahmā;
Without doubt, when those [qualities] have ceased to exist, through the accomplishment of the state beyond qualities (nirguṇa),
the attainment of kaivalya, which is the nature of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa), occurs.
An obstacle to knowledge:
subsequently, the knowledge of Nirguṇa Śiva, who is the very nature of the supreme Brahman-consciousness,
cannot be accomplished without the destruction of the perception of the phenomenal world, due to the residue of sin.
For worldly beings who are inert due to actions characterized by the delusion and doubt of duality,

the very cause for attaining liberation through association with the virtuous is indeed the initiation into virtuous action, meditation on Śiva, mental worship, and so forth; the absence of these alone is the obstacle to the knowledge of Brahman.
Regarding the three obstacles to liberation:
ignorance, doubt, and error are themselves the three obstacles to liberation.
Among these, ignorance is said to be the cause of the delusion of duality, namely the thought "I am not Brahman. Doubt is the mental state [wondering] "Am I Brahman or not?"
Doubt is to be dispelled by means of scripture (*śruti*) and reasoning (*yukti*). Scripture refers to the previously mentioned great sayings (*mahāvākya*) and so forth;

reasoning, however, consists in the fact that while it is logically consistent for the states of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) and being Brahman to coexist within a single Self due to the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the postulation of a distinct Self for every body would entail unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) such as "I am not the Lord."

It must be stated that there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [establishing] difference; for, just as in the case of the delusion that the moon is the size of a thumb, sublation (*bādha*) is possible regarding the knowledge produced by the scriptures. Thus, perception is not a means of valid cognition, nor is inference a means of valid cognition [for establishing non-difference], because the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses attributes such as the absence of omniscience—which is contrary to the omniscience that is an attribute of Brahman—and thus it is different from Brahman.

The property of the living being (*jīva*) characterized by the absence of omniscience—like that of a jar—is not contradictory to omniscience and so forth, because it is a property residing solely in the self (*ātman*), just like the property of being God (*īśvaratva*). Thus, the reason in the inference of non-difference is unestablished (*asiddha*). Since there is no contradiction due to its being non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), the living being is indeed Brahman; for it possesses selfhood (*ātmatva*), just like Brahman.
The means of valid cognition such as the Vedas and Smṛtis are merely restatements of differences established by perception;
and since restatements lack purposive intent regarding their own literal meaning. [Śloka]
I worship another deity, thinking, "He is one, and I am another."
He who knows that the object of knowledge is like a sacrificial animal, and likewise created within the existent;
There is fear because of their censure of the inquiry into the meaning of the Vedas.
If, through scripture and reasoning, I am Brahman, then to say that "I possess the previously established state of being a jīva" is itself a misconception.
This is the removal of the three obstacles.

Immediately following this, hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are, in their respective order, the three opposites of ignorance and the rest; among these, through the investigation of the sacred scriptures (*śruti-vicāra*), [one attains] the existence of firm conviction regarding the inner self (*pratyagātman*)— just as there is a firm conviction regarding the birth of a son and so forth.

"Listening" (*śravaṇa*) is said to be the activity conducive to ascertaining the intended meaning of the Upaniṣadic statements regarding the identity of the individual self (*jīva*) and Brahman; "reflection" (*manana*) is the successful contemplation of the reasoning concerning the subject matter of such scriptural revelation;
and [meditation] occurs when the object has been determined through both listening and reflection.
The continuous succession of streams of cognition characterized by mental modifications of the same class, unmixed with cognitions of a different class,
is called *nididhyāsana*; it is the auxiliary cause.

Immediately thereafter, through the knowledge of the meanings of the words contained within the Vedānta sentences arising from hearing (*śravaṇa*), the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Self is produced;
in this regard, first, by means of hearing, a pure knowledge in the form of indirect cognition (*parokṣa*) arises in two ways.

The venerable teacher Vācaspati Miśra holds that the direct realization of the Self arises through the mind aided by such means as hearing, reflection, and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*); whereas the venerable teacher Śrīpadācārya, the author of the *Vivaraṇa*, maintains that the direct realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self arises through the mere hearing of the Vedānta texts.

Their intention is as follows: knowledge produced by a sense organ (*indriya*) is not perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to inference (*anumiti*) and other such cognitions; nor is it "knowledge produced by a sense organ" in the sense of being delimited by the time that serves as the determinant of the state of being non-remote (*aparokṣa-janyatāvacchedaka*); nor is there such a thing as the universal (*jāti*) "perceptuality" (*pratyakṣatva*).

It might be argued that the genus *pratyakṣatva* (perceptuality) is not over-extended because it is delimited by the effectness of God’s perception through the relations of inherence and temporal connection; however, this cannot be maintained,
for the genus *anubhavatva* (experientiality) is simpler than that.

By means of the relations of inherence at the time [of perception], the relation of being the locus of a mediate cognition of its own substratum, and the relation of being the locus of difference from that [cognition], what is it that delimits the state of being produced by a sense organ? It is "perceptibility" (*pratyakṣatva*), because generality is simpler (*laghu*) and because there is no evidence for a genus of insentient things other than ignorance (*avidyā*). This is according to the rule that the suffixes *tva* and *tal* denote the state of being (*bhāva*).

Because it has as its primary meaning "existence" (sattā) as a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*), like the sūtra of the teacher Pāṇini, that [consciousness] is non-different from consciousness and is without support; as was stated by the venerable Bhartṛhari in the *Vākyapadīya*, in this verse:
Existence itself, being differentiated among cows and other things due to the difference in its relations, [is perceived as distinct].
That genus is the Great Self; they call it by suffixes such as -tva and -tal.

Therefore, the immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) of a cognition consists solely in its having an immediate object as its domain; and the so-called immediacy of an object is its identity with unobscured consciousness (*anāvṛta-saṃvit-tādātmyam*). For consciousness, however, which is already existent, its immediacy is simply its being the very essence of consciousness—as expressed by the scriptural statement "that which is directly perceived" (*sākṣād iti*). And that consciousness is indeed one alone. Is it not so?

If it is argued that direct perception (*aparokṣatva*) cannot exist because [the object] is not produced by contact with a sense-faculty (*indriya-saṃprayoga*), and since such contact consists of either conjunction (*saṃyoga*),

inherence in the conjoined (*saṃyukta-tādātmya*), inherence in what is inherent in the conjoined (*saṃyukta-tādātmya-tādātmya*), inherence (*tādātmya*), or inherence in what is inherent (*tādātmya-tādātmya*),
and none of these is present here— [we reply]: no, for this applies only to [ordinary] perception in general.

The mind is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because conjunction is not a cause [of cognition], because there is a deviation in the case of the perception of pleasure and so forth as well as dream-perception, and because the mind—being a transformation into cognition and a concomitant of all means of knowledge—lacks the status of being the instrument of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇatva*). [Furthermore,] it is like the self (*ātman*) or like *māyā*, since it is the material cause (*upādāna*) of cognition; and regarding the existence of *māyā*, there is proof.

The experience "I do not know the jar" is a direct valid cognition (*aparokṣapramāṇajñāna*) of the jar that does not produce the destruction of the jar, and it is the remover of the object of the experience "I do not know the jar," because it is a direct valid cognition of the jar,
like a direct valid cognition of the jar that does not produce the destruction of the jar.
Therefore, the knowledge whose object is the identity of Brahman and the Self, produced by the words of the Vedanta, is indeed immediate (aparokṣa),
because its object is immediately perceived; nor does this contradict the universally accepted usage in all philosophical systems that all knowledge produced by words is mediate (parokṣa).
Cognition through other words whose object is not directly perceived is indeed indirect (*parokṣa*);

even that produced by sentences such as "You are the tenth" is likewise [indirect]. By the word "primary" (*mukhya*), it is meant that hearing alone is primary; whereas reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are called "secondary" (*amukhya*) because they are auxiliaries (*sahakārin*) to hearing.

The division of auxiliary factors (*aṅgabhedah*) is as follows: in the case of the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) whose object is heaven, the sacrifice such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma*—which has become the instrument—is primarily the principal factor because it is heard [in scripture] as the instrument for the fruit; and according to the maxim that "that which is in proximity to what possesses a fruit is an auxiliary to that," [the other elements] are its auxiliaries.

Just as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering], the *agniṣṭomīya* animal sacrifice, and so forth are subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) by virtue of being non-primary and acting as auxiliaries, so it is in the present case as well. To the question "How so?", it follows that a lamp which reveals an object lacks the capacity for its function when in a flickering state. Subsequently—

Just as the movement of air is obstructed by tying a cloth over it, so too, when the mind is directed straight toward the wick of the lamp of consciousness, there occurs the presently manifesting state of *nididhyāsana*, which is like that very lamp burning brightly.
The next verse concerns the marks for determining the intended meaning of the Śruti.
The beginning and the conclusion, repetition, novelty, and fruit—these are the marks [of the purport].
Exegetical praise (arthavāda) and logical consistency (upapatti) are the indicators for determining the intended meaning (tātparya).
Such are the six kinds of indicators of purport that are conducive to the determination of the meaning of a treatise.
[Verse]
Before creation, the Supreme Brahman alone existed as the three worlds.
They suppressed the scent of the various internal distinctions within Brahman.
His speech begins with the realization of the bliss of undivided, singular essence.
Having brought about the dissolution of the world, which consists of name-and-form, into that very Self;
The internal [means] is the statement that brings about the realization of the identity of the inner self and the supreme self.
That which awakens to non-dual Brahman is of the nature of a concluding summary.
The opening and the conclusion constitute a single mark, not two.
The statement that repeatedly makes known the identity of the referents of the words "That" and "Thou."
Practice is said by the wise to be the state of being unapproachable by worldly measurement and the like;
it should be understood as "novelty" (*apūrvatā*) arising from the realization of oneness with Brahman;
and the attainment of all-knowledge is called the fruit by the learned.
Furthermore, [this applies] to the changeless Brahman, which is inwardly turned and firmly established.
The maxim "only one course of action should be contemplated" applies here.
Furthermore, [he possesses] the creation, dissolution, protection, and entry into the world.
And as for the rule: that statement which manifests the fivefold agency.

The statement of the actual fact is to be ascertained by the best among those who know the purposeful statements (*arthavāda*); furthermore, examples such as the navel of the belly and so forth are the logical justifications (*upapatti*). Thus, the scripture consisting of the six established marks is the instruction on Brahman.

Immediately following the causal complex of reflection (*manana*), reasoning, deliberation, and inference themselves serve as the aids to reflection; thus, according to the Sāṃkhya and other systems, there are multiple all-pervading selves (*ātman*), and [the inquiry concerns] those selves in their entirety within each individual body.

By the statement "there is a relationship," it is not possible to explain the persistence of experience by saying, "this body is the instrument of experience for this [self] alone and not for others. For if one were to say, "this body belongs to this [self] alone and not to others because it was produced for him through an abundance of merit (*sukṛta*)," then it would follow that others possess no merit and so forth.

When it was asked, "What [is the case]? immediately thereafter, and it was stated that the merit and so forth performed by him through the conceit (*abhimāna*) of his previous body belong to this very [person], [the objection was raised:

"Does that conceit not also belong to the many selves residing in the previous body? Or, if it does, then immediately after this, the fault of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) involving total confusion (*sāṃkarya*) would be unavoidable; how then can this be? When thus asked:

If it is argued that, since all selves are beginningless yet have been born, the distinction of experience is not possible immediately thereafter within the doctrine of a single self, and therefore one must resort to the doctrine of multiple selves—then [we reply]: this doubt regarding the establishment of experience arises equally in both views immediately after [the birth of selves]; thus, in the case of the doctrine of a single self...

It is logically consistent that the existence of diverse experiences is easily attained due to the multiplicity of the internal organ— which serves as the limiting adjunct— arising through its trembling, impurity, and so forth, according to the analogy of an object and its reflection; furthermore,
the definitions of perception and inference immediately following this [are found] in the *Khaṇḍana* and other works of Harṣamiśra Ācārya and others.

In works such as the *Khaṇḍanakhaḍyakhādya*, it is well known that by the statement "this exists," this section on the experience of pleasure is established; however, for fear of excessive length, Śrī Harṣamiśra did not provide a formal exposition, and in his treatise on refutation (*Khaṇḍana*), he rejected [the validity of] reasoning (*tarka*).
When it is asked, "How so?", there is this verse:
If there is doubt, there is contradiction; if there is no doubt, then all the more so.
There is contradiction, the suspicion of deafness, and reasoning; but from where does the limit of suspicion come?
When [the position] has been thus refuted by [the author of the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*] and others, they have defended [it] as follows:

regarding the [inference] "The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," when there is the doubt that "let the reason exist but let the probandum not exist," the tarka [is employed]: "If fire were not present, then smoke would also not be present."

The reasoning (*tarka*) consisting of the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) regarding the absence of fire and the absence of smoke has been shown; and *tarka* is of the nature of a superimposition (*āropa*) of the pervader produced by the apprehension of the pervaded. In that regard, when there is a suspicion of the lack of necessity (*aprayojakatva*) in the pervasion, if one were to present further *tarka*, it would be subject to the defect of suspicion, such as "it is the same there too," and "it is the same there too."
In that case, the establishment of the fundamental pervasion (*mūlavyāpti*) would not even occur, and thus there would be the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

When there is doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in some instances, the non-arising of doubt occurs either due to the absence of the recollection of the two alternatives (*koṭi*) and so forth, or in other cases through reasoning (*tarka*); thus, there is no infinite regress. If the relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between smoke and fire did not exist, then smoke—

If smoke could exist even without fire, then it would not be produced by fire; and if there were doubt regarding its lack of causal necessity (*aprayojaka-śaṅkā*) even in that case, one would not engage in activity toward fire for the sake of obtaining smoke. Thus, out of fear of the "staff" of contradicting one's own purpose, the relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva*) between the two must be accepted—such is the investigation of *tarka*.

In the section concerning the experience of bliss, the "solid" [nature] was set aside. It has been stated that the relationship between the Lord (Īśvara) and the individual soul (jīva) exists by way of the relation between an original image and its reflection; that [relationship] is obtained when the limiting adjunct (upādhi) exists.

That limiting adjunct, however, is Māyā, and she is the object of disagreement regarding the nature of ignorance (avidyā), which is the knowledge derived from the means of valid cognition (pramāṇajñāna).

It is preceded by another entity that is distinct from its own prior absence, which obscures its own object, is superimposed upon the substrate of its own object, and is sublated by itself, because it is either non-manifest or partially manifest, or because its object is a real entity obscured by a superimposed veil.

The demonstration that [the knowledge of the probandum] is like the instrumental cognition regarding an object situated in a room, which dispels the delusion caused by the darkness therein, and so forth, has been set aside as being too difficult; furthermore, the definition of inference is also to be known through the knowledge of the definitions of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the subject-ness of the locus (*pakṣatā*), and so on.
The five yogas of nididhyāsana are said to be mantra-yoga, sparśa-yoga, bhāva-yoga, abhāva-yoga, and mahā-yoga; among these,
[the first] is through the contemplation of mantras such as the *praṇava*.

The dissolution of the mind within the Supreme Self (paramātman) is called *mantrayoga*. Furthermore, when that *mantrayoga*, conjoined with the mind and the vital breath (*pavana*), unites as one and proceeds through the *suṣumnā* path to the base of the spine (*mūlādhāra*), and finally dissolves into the splendor of the Supreme Self residing in the head—that very dissolution is called *sparśayoga*. Thus it is described.

Having meditated upon the singular Vairāja form of the divine Śambhu, which is praised by all the sages, whose head is heaven, whose two ears are the quarters of space, whose two eyes are the moon and the sun, whose mouth is fire, whose navel is the earth, and whose feet are the moving worlds; ||| [then...]
Or rather, his divine form is to be visualized with a body immeasurable due to the ornaments of weapons grasped directly by his arms.
Immediately thereafter, having dissolved each individual part among those parts one by one,

the dissolution of the mind into the Brahman that exists as the mere reality of the remaining whole is called *bhāvayoga*. [Cūlikā] Furthermore, [the yoga] which impels the eyes, speech, and other faculties toward conversation and the like, which produce the intellect desired by all living beings...

He who transcends the means of knowledge such as inference— which possess the skill of making objects known, including the various insentient things that are distinct from the Vedas and are celebrated by those wise in all the worlds, and which operate within the sphere of instruments characterized by speech, ears, and other senses.

The Supreme Brahman—praised by the five forms that perform the creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace of the universe; transcending the association with limiting adjuncts such as *māyā* which oppose the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that conforms to innate bliss equal to a waveless ocean; [the Supreme Brahman].
Thus, when the mind is dissolved, the yoga of non-existence (abhāvayoga) indeed manifests once again. [Verse]
In the pair of the arising and passing away of the world, and in the states of the knower and the known.
Since there is no loss of its own nature, it is represented as having the single form of existence.
The dissolution of the mind in the sign of Brahman, which is the inner self, is the great yoga.
Regarding the three obstacles:

immediately following [the mention of] past, present, and future obstacles, these very three—past obstacles, present obstacles, and future obstacles—are the three obstacles to the direct realization of the Self; among them, with respect to liberation...
Even after renouncing all attachments, attaining a venerable guru, and performing such acts as hearing the scriptures,

there remains a lingering relish for the experience of the beautiful qualities— such as beauty, youth, and elegance— of the wife and other objects previously accepted during the householder stage of life.
Having arrived again and again by means of the fruit of past formations (*saṃskāra*), dwelling in the mind and giving rise to anxiety at every step,
it is called "the obstructor of reality" (*bhūtapratibandhakarī*) even while existing, because it fails to bring about the direct realization (*ātmasākṣātkāra*) of the self.
Furthermore, [it is said in] the verse:
One who is dull-witted, who delights in the company of living beings, and who is likewise attached to sense objects;
Fallacious reasoning, conceit, and fickleness—these are of six kinds.
And for whom these exist when there is an investigation into reality.
It does not produce the direct realization of that [Self]; such is the established conclusion.
This great obstacle, existing in the form of an impediment, stands before me.
If it has not perished without first attaining another birth, then indeed [it does not perish].
Due to the distinction of having long since commenced [the practice], and through the desire for the world of Brahmā and other realms.
Even for one who possesses knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas, due to the agitation caused by these two defects...
In this case, the impossibility of direct realization would constitute a future obstacle.
Immediately following the means for removing obstacles, knowledge (*jñāna*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and cessation (*uparati*) become the primary means to conquer the three types of bondage.
Regarding the practice performed in one's final birth, as to how that practice is carried out:
I shall explain, one by one and in sequence, the three characteristics which are precisely the cause, the essential nature, and the effect of that [reality].
When it is asked, "What is the characteristic of knowledge? the answer is that hearing [the teachings] and so forth are the causes of knowledge;
the discrimination between the identity and the difference of the superimposition of the Self and the ego-sense constitutes its essential nature.
Immediately thereafter, the very state of being the witness to the transmigratory existence residing within the ego-sense becomes the task to be accomplished.
Regarding the definition of detachment (*vairāgya*):

immediately following that, the very cause of detachment is the perception of defects such as impermanence in objects like women and the like; its essential nature (*svarūpa*), however, is the renunciation of those objects in whatever manner possible.
The very absence of attainment is the effect.
Regarding the characteristic of cessation (*uparati*):

immediately following [the definition of yoga], the very cause of cessation is the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) consisting of restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), and so forth. Its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the attainment of one-pointedness within the inner sphere of the mind.
Furthermore, in external ritual action, the very absence of direct orientation [toward the deity] is what must be accomplished.
The limits of knowledge and the other [perfections] are as follows:

among them, the limit of knowledge (*jñāna*) is the firm conviction that "Brahman alone is myself," just as one who has attained the state of identifying the body with the self [regards the body as the self]; the limit of [the power of] attaining the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) and so forth is the disregard for it like a blade of grass.

The limit of dispassion: If it is argued that for them, the three—knowledge, dispassion, and cessation—are accomplished, wherein the limit of cessation is simply the forgetting of all effects, like deep sleep, and this constitutes the cause of liberation; [then we respond: for them...
When it is asked, "How does that become the fruit of great austerity?", [the answer is:
if there is an absence of ignorance while the true state of both dispassion (*vairāgya*) and cessation (*uparati*) is fully present, liberation (*mukti*) does not occur for him;
rather, he attains the higher world (*ūrdhvaloka*), which serves as the abode of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). However, for one who possesses the presence of knowledge (*jñāna*), [liberation occurs].

Just as when the branch at the top of a tree breaks, a person standing there falls even though he has no desire to fall— due to the absence of dispassion and cessation [of karma]— so too, at the end of the body, liberation occurs;
it is established that there is only the experience of suffering produced by *prārabdha* [karma].
The sequence of the seven stages:

immediately following [the first], there is the desire for bliss, reflection, subtle mental engagement, attachment, the attainment of being, the cultivation of the categories of objects, and progression through the fourth [dhyāna].
"Aḥ! There are seven stages of knowledge; having become deluded regarding them, I exist [in this state].
Therefore, that which is called *śubhecchā* (the desire for the auspicious) is the realization that 'this must be known through scripture and the guru.
Furthermore, when there arises an inclination toward right conduct due to a slight degree of detachment produced by the guru and the scriptures, that very state is called *vicāraṇā* (investigation)."

Immediately following this, through the power of the desire for bliss and discernment, the very abandonment of attachment to sense objects is called *tanumānasī*; by the force of practicing the three aforementioned stages,
one perceives the entire waking world as being like a dream, [realizing it is] not of the Self.

The continuous contemplation of being the Mother of all (sanmātṛtvānusaṃdhāna) is called the attainment of Being (satvāpatti). Having realized the non-appearance of the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), the state in which only the pure consciousness of the Self remains, like deep sleep, is called absorption (saṃsakti). Immediately thereafter, through the dissolution of all latent impressions (vāsanā), it is the very state of being merged in the nature of Bliss, as if in a profound slumber.

When it is not said whether there is or is not an objective entity (padārtha-bhāvanā) above [this state], that which exists as the non-dual state (advaita-pada) in the form of pure consciousness (kevala-jñapti), devoid of both egoism (ahaṃkṛti) and non-egoism (nirahaṃkṛti), and abiding in an open space like an empty jar—
existing through its internal and external emptiness— is precisely what is called "attaining the fourth state" (turyagāmī).
Furthermore, the six samādhis— which follow upon the cessation of those [perceptions] and are called "pervasion by the visible," "pervasion by sound," and "non-conceptual"—
are, through their division into external and internal, the six samādhis; among these, within the collection of objects such as jars and so forth:

Whatever object one takes as a focus, having set aside its two illusory components consisting of name and form, and then unites within it the three Brahman-components of existence, luminosity, and bliss— which are the essence of being, consciousness, and bliss— that state, characterized by the permeation of the external object of perception, is called *savikalpa-samādhi*.

Furthermore, the very act of meditating on Brahman as being of the nature of indivisible, real, conscious, blissful, and non-dual— characterized by the interpenetration of external words— is called *savikalpa-samādhi*. Subsequently,
through the power of practicing these two types of samādhi, when the mind becomes immersed in the savoring of the bliss of Brahman that has arisen, [that is known as nirvikalpa-samādhi].
That which exists in a state of immobility, like a waveless ocean,
is itself external non-conceptual samādhi; immediately thereafter, the very objects of desire, volitions, and so forth residing in the mind become its own visible field.
The continuous contemplation of "I am the Witness" itself is the *savikalpa-samādhi* characterized by the internal penetration of the object of perception;

furthermore, the act of contemplating that one's own nature is indeed the non-dual self-luminous reality of unattached Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*) is called the internal penetration of sound, which is known as *savikalpa-samādhi*.
Furthermore, by directing the taste of one's own such experience toward the two remaining objects—the seen and the heard—one abides in a state of motionlessness like a lamp placed in a windless spot;
this alone is called internal nirvikalpa-samādhi. [Śloka]
The great yogi passes his time through six types of meditative absorption.
Wherever his mind goes, there his concentrations abide.
The four fruits of knowledge; a verse.
The absence of suffering and the attainment of all desires constitute the state of having accomplished what was to be done.
For this fourfold nature of the fruit consists precisely in the attainment of that which is to be attained.

Among those, the absence of suffering exists in two ways, distinguished by this world and the next: in the gross body, there are ugliness, foul odor, and diseases; in the subtle body, there are desire, anger, and so forth, as they are perceived; and in the causal body, there are the latent impressions (*saṃskāras*) which serve as the seeds for mental afflictions and physical ailments.

In this world, there is suffering consisting of the threefold affliction; in these, [suffering ceases] through the knowledge of the inner self— which is non-dual and distinct from the body and so forth that consist of the effects of false selfhood and illusion— insofar as it is devoid of the ultimate relationship between enjoyer and enjoyed.
For the knower, the absence of connection with those three types of suffering is called the "absence of suffering in this world.
The anxiety, "How is merit to be attained? How is sin to be warded off?
constitutes the suffering of the next world; in that regard, after the attainment of perfect knowledge, [sin] is like water on a lotus leaf.
