For the knower, there is no stain from the two types of action; just as fire exists within wood yet the wood and other such things cease to exist when the fire is present, so the man of discrimination abides in the worldly transaction of the two types of action, yet when that transaction ceases, he is like those beasts or birds in the sky who are not affected by the flames of a forest fire.
In the same way, for the wise, this [world] cannot be bound by good or evil deeds and so forth;
therefore, the absence of anxiety and knowledge [of such bonds], as well as the absence of suffering in the next world, are spoken of.
Furthermore, the attainment of desires—
ranging from the universal monarch endowed with all sovereignty up to Hiraṇyagarbha—
are each to be regarded as hundredfold greater in bliss than the preceding one; yet even all these are objects of indifference for the discerning person.

Immediately following this, by the statement that "all joys are portions of Brahman fully known by the knower," the establishment of his indivisible bliss (*akhaṇḍānanda*) occurs; that which constitutes this is what is called the attainment of all desires (*sarvakāmāpti*).

Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra the great sage, Durvāsas, Nārada, and others who are leaders among those liberated while living— these various manifestations arising from this very way of life serve as illustrations here.
The distinction between the knower and the ignorant:

Immediately following this, when it is asked what the difference is between the knower and the ignorant if both accept the experience of *prārabdha* karma, [the answer is] that it is like the difference between an outcaste (*vrātya*) and a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), based on whether or not they have abandoned the study of the Vedas.

Even though there is a difference [between them], just as there is an absence of difference regarding food, sleep, and so forth, a distinction certainly exists between the ignorant and the wise due to their connection with or lack of connection to the "heart-knot" (hṛdayagranthi);
it is indeed accepted that there is no difference in the state of their experience.
Regarding the possibility of the effort toward one's own destruction:

immediately thereafter, when the attainment of Brahman occurs through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the state of being a living individual (*jīvatva*) dissolves—just as [the fear] vanishes upon seeing that it was merely a tiger. If this is so, how can there be a "living individual" for the sake of one's own destruction?
When it is said that [the soul] "proceeds," just as in the world one may, out of a desire for divinity,
accept the relinquishing of human status in relation to Bhṛgu, Agni, the current of the Gaṅgā, and so forth,
so too does that individual soul, through the knowledge of reality, [accept the relinquishing of its limited state] in order to abide as Brahman in the form of the inner self.
It is well known that he exists while accepting his own destruction.
Praise of the Liberated-while-Living:

It has been stated that only that person who possesses the power to bestow curses and favors—like Vyāsa and others—is a knower of reality, and no other; such power, however, is the fruit of austerity (tapas).

It should be understood that [knowledge alone] does not constitute the fruit of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Immediately following this, since there is a scriptural authority stating that austerity (*tapas*) is indeed the primary means for the knowledge of reality when it has arisen in such a manner, one might ask how the knowledge of reality can belong to one devoid of austerity; [the answer concerns] curses and so forth.

It can be inferred that for those such as Vyāsa and others, true knowledge of reality arises through disinterested austerity (*niṣkāma-tapas*) as opposed to the interested austerity (*sakāma-tapas*) that serves as a causal factor; furthermore,
when it is said that they possess two capacities for the attainment of true knowledge, it implies that they possess both types of austerity.

There are two capacities of knowledge. Immediately thereafter, as he practices each specific form of austerity, each corresponding perfection arises; thus, there is no contradiction. It is said that immediately thereafter, all those devoted to ritual action (kriyāniṣṭha) revile the knower of reality (tattvajñānin), who is devoid of ritual injunctions and lacks the capacity for curses and the like.

Even though they have reached the culmination of their practice (*kriyāniṣṭha*), there is still censure by the vulgar who are greedy for sense-objects; thus, there is no inequality [between them]. Furthermore, when it is asked, "What loss is there for the cultured (*śiṣṭa*) who have reached the culmination of practice, even if they are rejected by those greedy for sense-objects? [the answer is] the body...

Thus, by refuting the notion that the self is the agent of intelligent actions, it becomes truly accurate that there is no loss whatsoever for the knower of reality; furthermore, by the statement "he is liberated while living and extraordinary," it is shown that even though he remains in the state of either a knower or a non-knower due to the force of *prārabdha*, he is like the wind.
Like the sky amidst layers of clouds— both those resting upon it and those supported by it— it remains eternally pure. Furthermore,
even while accepting enjoyments such as garlands and sandalwood paste offered by invisible attendants,
it remains possessed of longing for another, like an unchaste woman who has attained sexual pleasure with her own husband.

Furthermore, although he remains silent while appearing like one who is ignorant yet actually possessing knowledge of the arts (*kalā*), he becomes indolent amidst the sphere of the articulated speech (*vaikharī*) of fabricated scriptural statements; thus, it is said regarding him when he engages in much talk concerning the current commands.

Furthermore, the intention of the Veda—which culminates in the non-duality of Truth (satyādvaita) contained within its hidden purport—becomes manifest when the Teacher, though remaining established [in that state], instructs his disciples by means of the statement: "The Self is eternally liberated. Having reached the firm conviction that the relationship between the knower and the known consists of the construction of Māyā, the Guru [speaks] like a voice from the sky.

He becomes free from egoism; furthermore, though speaking inappropriately like one who is mad, he becomes one who delights in the Self, devoid of the sense of duality. Thus it is said that, at the conclusion of sexual union, the speech of a couple intensely attached to passion becomes a matter that cannot be described in words.

Just like one possessed by a *piśāca* spirit, even while walking about, he has become established in the nature of the One Fullness; thus, through this, his contemplation becomes unattainable, like that of a lover in separation. Furthermore, being one who experiences the loss of a son, he grieves like a common village man—this is precisely what [the text] means.
Without even reaching the realization that all the sense-faculties are of the nature of a portion of Brahman,
he experiences the flavor of compassion toward the objects and qualities of the sense-faculties and so forth— which have been restrained— amidst the state of an imagined practitioner; then,
laughing boisterously at the amusement of beholding various distorted forms, he utters a loud laugh (*aṭṭahāsa*).

Establishing that the conventional discourse of diverse merits, demerits, and so forth is indeed real, there arises a parodic critique of systems such as Mīmāṃsā; furthermore, by the statement "even while remaining like a libertine through passion for women,
he has become one whose nature is entirely full," he becomes an experiencer of his own innate bliss.
Like an enemy, what man can be brought to such torment by anger alone that one would place trust in him—

like a fire that burns a field— for the sake of attaining the distinguished fruit of liberation, which is the state of disembodied isolation (*videhakaivalya*)? One must rely on him for that attainment.

Immediately following that, when it is asked how the attainment of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*) occurs— at whatever time and in whatever place, without reaching any physical body, by existing as the very nature of Brahman which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*)— the *Cūrṇikā* explains it thus:

In any preeminent person who possesses the excellence born from a thorough mastery of various scriptures, who is foremost in the skill of cultivating the Vedānta system, and who is endowed with a constant desire for eternally pure liberation; and through whose steadfastness and performance of obligatory rites— which bestow the grace of the Supreme Lord— there has arisen a continuous succession of *apūrva* (unseen spiritual merit).

It is endowed with the destruction of millions of rows of sins produced by the succession of those [previous] dharmas; it is brilliantly shining through the abundance of mental purity being generated by the destruction of sin;
and it is auspicious due to the fruits of good and evil in this world and the next arising from that mental purity.
To the one who is skilled in the fortitude and excellence born from the dispassion toward sense-objects arising from perceiving the defects of worldly existence;
to the one who possesses all-enduring patience manifested through the longing for liberation characterized by the pervasive bliss born of detachment from sense-objects.

In this place crowded with the multitude of those who find delight in the inner self, as manifested through the practice of yoga revealed in the compositions of Jālandhara and others— [a practice] which arises from the cessation of those karmas that cause one to reach the very limits of the world of Brahmā.

It is a lake whose waters consist of the investigation of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*), which are like pearls from the ocean of the four Vedas that establish the identity of Brahman and the Self born of delight in the inner Self; it is filled with the various waves of reality consisting of the bubbles of many millions of cosmic eggs produced by the non-dual knowledge arising therefrom,
and it possesses the tortoises of various pleasures and the like within the mire of suffering.

In that which shines with the non-perception of the delusion of duality— produced by the destruction of the ocean of supreme illusion, which is continuously extended by the succession of beings such as insects—
and in which there occurs the abandonment of the notions of auspicious and inauspicious born from not seeing that [duality], resulting in the attainment of the loss of passion and hatred;

In that [state], which is capable of effecting the liberation from all fetters by producing the cessation of the divine state dependent upon the destruction of merit and demerit— [a state] appearing as the negation of injunctions and prohibitions;
and which is the locus of the final, most excellent station produced therein, free from rebirth, and the clamor of all scriptures.

The priceless state of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*), which is established through the grace of the scriptures and the teacher, and is determined by the realization that the impressions of names, classes, actions, and attainments—which terminate in mere discursive speech—do not constitute the domain of mind or speech; this state, whose nature is eternal bliss, unfolds [within].

[Thus ends the work] of the venerable [author], who has crossed the ocean of words, sentences, and means of valid knowledge, and who is the one who drank the milk from the womb of the illustrious Harapura-Ñajarāja.
Composed by Śrī Liṅgarāja, who is like the moon in the western sky, a pearl released from the oyster-shell of Mother Cāmā’s womb,
whose own mind acts as a bee at the lotus-feet of the glorious Umāramaṇa,
and whose own glance is endowed with compassion extended for the protection of those who have sought refuge.
In the *Vivekacintāmaṇivivaraṇa* composed by Śrī Liṅgarāja— which serves as a crown for all learned men—
the first chapter, which illuminates all subjects beginning with the Vedas, is completed.
Salutations to Śrī Śiva.
[Now the Second Chapter] Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. The path of the Śiva-siddhānta, as previously described.
Consciousness is eternal, peaceful, beyond the ether, and stainless.
Salutation to that venerable Guru who has transcended sound, the point, and the energy-portion.

Thus, having established the primary meaning of the Vedas and Shastras in Prakrit, I have composed this for the sake of those who are qualified; let it be so. Now, I shall describe in detail, with an attentive mind, the path of the Shiva-Siddhanta, which is higher than the highest and of the nature previously described.
It must be understood alone. ||2|| When it is attained by the excellent practitioner, there is constant bliss that arises;

through this investigation of the scripture. ||3|| If one asks how that was stated, then within those very scriptures of established doctrine (siddhānta), it was said, "The fruit shall be manifest to the world," thinking thus. ||4||

The cause for the manifestation of trust is through that [realization]; for its sake, wisdom is described. How can one speak of both the categories of the Self? ||5|| It has been stated with profound depth by means of various names; if one asks, "What are their characteristics?"—then it is said:
The Gāruḍa [Tantra] on the right, the Bhūta [Tantra] on the left, and the Catuṣka-tantra-vidhāna.

In their place: ||7|| Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta—these are said to be the fourfold modes of worship for the form of Brahmā. ||8|| [The powers of] snake-charm, healing, victory over enemies, alchemy, and the driving away of evil spirits; by these—
Now begins the section on existence: the sequence [of chapters], 9: the Gāruḍa [tantra] concerning the discourse on killing, including mantras and medicinal herbs.
Thus, it is established by the power of such logical application. ||10||
There are differences in the scriptures, as well as contradictions; there are divergences in established doctrines. Which one is renowned, and of what nature?
It is said as follows: 1. Kāmikāgama, 2. Yogajāgama, 3. Ciṃtyāgama, 4.
Kāraṇāgama, 5. Ajitāgama, 6. Dīptāgama, 7. Sūkṣmāgama, 8. Sahasrāgama, 9. Aṃśumānāgama, 10. Suprabhedāgama, 11. Vijayāgama, 12. Viśvāsāgama, 13. Svayaṃbhuvāgama, and 14. Analāgama.

14 Vīrāgama, 15 Rauravāgama, 16 Makutāgama, 17 Vimalāgama, 18 Candrajñānāgama, 19 Bimbāgama, 20 Prodgitāgama, 21 Lalitāgama, 22 Siddhāgama, 23 Santānāgama, 24 Śarvoktāgama, 25 Pārameśvarāgama, 26 Kiraṇāgama, 27 Vātulāgama. (11) Thus.
The number of Śivāgamas is twenty-eight, having been previously enumerated as the Kāmika and so forth.
From the mouths of Sadāśiva, they were produced in succession; thus the Āgamas were known. 12.
The group of five with the face of Sadyojāta; the group of five with the face of Vāmadeva; the group of five with the face of Aghora;
the group of five with the face of Tatpuruṣa; [the group of five] with the face of Īśāna; and the group of eight with the faces of those [others]. 13.
The principal ones have been produced; in their place [are] Kāmika and the others, ending with Suprabodha. 14.
The ten Āgamas are certain; they are the divisions of Śiva, free from the Brahmanical [Vedic] path.
Non-existent in Nirvāṇa, present in the Urala, and existing from Vijayā up to Vāyuta. ||15||
The eighteen Āgamas are the Brahmayāmala; the Rudrabheda is the sixteenth.
The descent of the Āgamas:
Śiva, Rudra, and Āpāsa. Regarding the origin of the Āgamas—how they all came to be—if one were to say so:
17. From the mouth of Sadyojāta comes the Kāmika Āgama; therein, the Praṇava was first understood.
By her, the three times were traversed; by her, the face was taken as the gain. 18.
The first [treatise] born of yoga is named Sudhā; from that, the principal [work] was produced by his arms.
The *Tayāmukha* was known by Viśekhā; it was first illuminated by Vibhu.
From that [source], the one called *Yoga* was obtained; its primary *siddhānta* was known by Ambikā. The *Kāraṇāgama* was first [revealed] in the *Kāraṇākhyāna*; from that [source]...
From that [source], all the arts and dharmas arose; from that, Prajāpati was born. 21.
The first Śiva is Ajitāgama; from him arose Suśiva; even more excellent than he is Taya-pāsa-va.
Having realized the state of the Imperishable (acyuta), [he attained it]. From the mouth of Vāmadeva, the radiant scripture emerged;
that was the first brought forth by Īśa. From that, the circumambulation (parikrama) was fashioned as the triple form (trimūrti).
23. By her words, he was known for certain by the fire-god Viśvakarman.

The Dharma of Āgama ||24|| Explanation of the Sūkṣmāgama: First, Vaiśravaṇa [appeared] in Sūkṣma and Tayāmukha; from him came Prabhañjana, who understood the dharma ||25|| Aṃśumān’s Āgama was first; then Ambu...

The waters were fierce; he approached them according to the Āgama dharma. Having obtained the *aurasa* [son], he was the first Rudra among the thousand who came from that [source]; more excellent than those waters was Bhīmarudra.

In that [work], the investigation of Dharma is at its beginning. Having understood it, [it was said]: "First, the *Suprabodha-āgama* was investigated; it was heard from the ten directions by Vighneśvara at its beginning. Then, from him, Śaśin learned it with reverence. Thus are the ten Āgamas, a division of the one called Śiva.
Thus it was said.

First, Vijayā, whose face is not terrible (Aghoramukhī), emerged from Āṇika; she was brought forth by Rudra from the Āgama. By means of her supreme mouth, which is beginningless and without beginning, she was fashioned. Nandīśvara is her *kalā*. 29.
